candidates.title: Multi-dimensional hierarchical temporal alignment for improved temporal commonsense reasoning in large language models
candidates.abstract: Benefiting from recent advances in generative AI and large language models (LLMs), current LLM-driven AI systems are rapidly reshaping how we reason, plan, and make decisions. Yet endowing these systems with human-like temporal intelligence (e.g., understanding and comparing events across time) remains largely unresolved. To address this gap, we introduce a novel Multi-dimensional Hierarchical Temporal Alignment framework (denoted as MHTA), of which the core idea is to effectively ground the temporal alignment of an LLM in both event-specific and cross-event real-world temporal commonsense knowledge. Specifically, we first frame the temporal space as a multi-dimensional hierarchical space, where each dimension comprises its own set of temporal units. Building on this formulation, we curate an initial burn-in dataset in which annotations are constructed to reflect real-world human temporal commonsense in accordance with our defined temporal space. Based on the initial burn-in dataset, we propose two complementary fine-tuning objectives: (i) Grounding the temporal alignment in event-specific temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved through a novel hierarchy-preserving Wasserstein loss, and (ii) Grounding the temporal alignment in cross-event temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved via a margin-adaptive triplet loss. To evaluate the effectiveness of MHTA, we conduct extensive experiments on three representative benchmarks (MCTACO, DurationQA, and TimeDial). For example, on the MCTACO dataset, MHTA improves Mistral-7B by 6.0% in accuracy and 10.3% in exact match, and improves DeepSeek-LLM-7B by 5.4% in accuracy and 9.8% in exact match. Combined with different backbones, MHTA surpasses nearly all baselines across the three benchmarks and exceeds the performance of advanced models such as GPT-4o on MCTACO and DurationQA. These results demonstrate that MHTA provides consistent gains in temporal commonsense reasoning across diverse LLM backbones.

candidates.title: Stateful Monitor-Router-Rollback Regulation for Robust Functional Recovery in Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Prompt injection can divert large language model (LLM) agents from authorized objectives and contaminate subsequent conversational context. We investigate a deterministic Monitor-Router-Rollback (MRR) supervisory controller designed to detect suspicious instructions, constrain execution paths, and reconstruct trusted task context after exposure. The evaluation uses 400 matched attack scenarios, four attack families, three locally served models (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 32B, and Mistral-Nemo 12B), seven completed defense conditions, and four recorded phases yielding 33,600 completed model-scenario-defense-phase observations. Our findings demonstrate model-dependent robustness improvements—particularly for Llama 3.1 8B, where automated utility increases from 36.00% to 81.25% under MRR—while establishing rigorous methodological boundaries regarding semantic adjudication, component attribution, and repeated snapshot reconstruction.

candidates.title: A Review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Architectural Evolution, Key Breakthroughs, and Vertical-Domain Practices
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on massive pretraining based on the Transformer architecture and show significant emergent effects in general tasks. However, the nature of their statically parameterized knowledge causes vertical-domain applications to face three core bottlenecks: knowledge hallucination, delayed timeliness, and loss in long contexts. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) realizes the decoupling of computational logic and factual memory through the paradigm of “retrieve first and generate afterward”. It can dynamically inject domain knowledge without fine-tuning and has become a mainstream technical path for the implementation of trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI). This study systematically reviews the evolution of RAG technology from 2024 to 2026, from Naive RAG to Advanced RAG, Modular RAG, and graph-enhanced RAG. It analyzes in depth the breakthrough progress of four key technologies, namely hybrid retrieval, multimodal document parsing, generation control, and lightweight deployment. Combined with typical application cases in complex equipment manufacturing, energy and power, public services, and other fields, it explains the engineering value of RAG. Finally, it discusses the evaluation system, existing limitations, and future trends, providing a reference for academic research and practical implementation of RAG technology.

candidates.title: Layanan Informasi Peraturan Akademik Berbasis Chatbot Telegram Menggunakan Pendekatan Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Academic Regulation Information Service Based on a Telegram Chatbot Using a Retrieval-Augmented Generation Approach
candidates.abstract: Peraturan akademik merupakan pedoman penting dalam penyelenggaraan pendidikan tinggi. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengembangkan chatbot berbasis Telegram untuk layanan informasi peraturan akademik menggunakan pendekatan Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) di Politeknik Negeri Padang dengan memanfaatkan basis pengetahuan institusi yang telah terverifikasi. Sistem dikembangkan menggunakan PHP dengan framework Laravel dan basis data PostgreSQL yang didukung oleh ekstensi pgvector untuk penyimpanan embedding. Model gemini-embedding-001 digunakan untuk mengubah dokumen peraturan akademik menjadi representasi vektor sehingga memungkinkan proses temu kembali dokumen berdasarkan kemiripan semantik, sedangkan model gemini-2.5-flash digunakan untuk menghasilkan respons berdasarkan konteks peraturan yang berhasil ditemukan. Basis pengetahuan sistem terdiri atas Peraturan Akademik Politeknik Negeri Padang yang mencakup 18 bab dan 75 pasal. Evaluasi proses temu kembali menggunakan 15 pertanyaan uji memperoleh nilai Precision sebesar 0,7467, Recall sebesar 0,9667, dan Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) sebesar 0,9333. Selanjutnya, evaluasi pembangkitan jawaban menggunakan 10 pertanyaan uji dengan metode Large Language Model (LLM)-as-a-judge menghasilkan skor relevansi rata-rata sebesar 4,90 pada chatbot berbasis RAG, lebih tinggi dibandingkan chatbot tanpa RAG yang memperoleh skor sebesar 3,20. Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa pendekatan RAG efektif dalam menyediakan layanan informasi akademik yang cepat, akurat, dan mudah diakses.

candidates.title: Multimodal Large Language Model-Enabled Healthcare Information System Design
candidates.abstract: Cross-border health-care information systems often struggle to deliver culturally embedded medical knowledge—such as traditional Chinese medicine—to international users with varying health literacy, due to fragmented architecture and weak semantic alignment across languages. This study proposed a tripartite framework built on the Qwen2.5 Vision-Language model at the 7-billion parameter scale, integrating cross-lingual perception, domain knowledge enhancement, and terminology alignment to support multimodal health-care information processing. A bidirectional label-matching feedback mechanism and an entropy-weighted coupling coordination model were developed to quantify system-level synergy. Using 12,642 dissemination records and 7,869 health-care cases (2019–2025), the proposed system outperformed OpenAI's generative pretrained transformer 4o mini by 7.1 points on average across core indicators, with coupling coordination rising from 0.409 to 0.716 and regional synergy gains of 0.382 in Southeast Asia. The framework achieved a 39.2% retention rate in full-chain service conversion and over 83% adaptability for low-health-literacy users.

candidates.title: Large language models in geospatial science
candidates.abstract: Purpose Large language models are opening new ways to work with geospatial data, from asking questions about places to building analytical workflows. This study aims to examine how these applications fit together and what they suggest about the developing role of LLMs in geospatial science. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of 55 studies was conducted, covering GIScience and related spatial applications. Dictionary-based coding, supported by manual review, was combined with term frequency–inverse document frequency analysis and non-negative matrix factorisation to examine research roles, tasks and themes. Comparisons between core GIScience and adjacent fields helped place the overall patterns in context. Findings Benchmarking was the most common research role (41.8%), followed by multimodal interpretation (20.0%). Across the literature, two complementary directions emerge: using language models to organise geospatial operations and using vision-language models to interpret spatial observations. The abstracts place particular emphasis on methods, while the thematic analysis connects general GIS evaluation with code generation, remote sensing and applied spatial reasoning. Practical implications The synthesis points to the value of combining flexible language interfaces with established GIS computation. Practical evaluation should consider how a system turns a request into a verified spatial result, including the time and expert involvement needed to complete that process. Originality/value By bringing GIScience and adjacent spatial research into one analytical framework, the review shows how model capabilities, data representations and external tools contribute to geospatial workflows. This perspective offers a basis for comparing systems and identifying productive connections between research communities.

candidates.title: From Harness Optimization to Recursive Self-Improvement: A Survey of Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Language-model agents rely on harnesses that govern tool use, context, memory, and execution. Understanding automated harness revision requires connecting improvement methods to the reusable functionality they produce. This survey examines three linked perspectives: improvement workflows, recursive scope, and concrete modifications across task domains. We compare search strategies, memory management, edit guidance, and integration with model training, and use an existing five-level framework to distinguish harness optimization from recursive self-improvement. Across coding, reasoning and information processing, interactive and embodied tasks, and visual tasks, we trace reported changes from starting capabilities to outcomes. Our synthesis identifies repairs at model–environment interfaces, cases where added tools and context fail to help, and conditions constraining recovery reuse. Cross-domain analogies motivate, rather than establish, transfer. We distinguish task-performance gains from improved subsequent optimization and identify priorities in reliable evaluation, attribution, transfer, and safety.

candidates.title: Correctness and Completeness of a Multimodal Large Language Model in the Diagnosis and Treatment Recommendations for Proximal Femoral Fractures
candidates.abstract: Background and Objectives: To compare the diagnostic and therapeutic performance of a multimodal large language model (GPT) with that of two human evaluators in proximal femoral fracture (PFF) assessment, focusing on correctness and completeness. Materials and Methods: A consecutive series of 250 PFFs was reconstructed into standardized clinical scenarios including radiographs and structured clinical data. Each case was independently evaluated by a trauma fellow, a second-year orthopaedic resident, and GPT. Responses were scored for diagnostic and treatment correctness and completeness. Severe treatment errors were predefined as category-changing mismatches, failure to recognize an existing implant, or incorrect laterality. Results: Fully correct diagnoses were achieved in 97.2% of cases by the fellow, 44.8% by the resident, and 14.0% by GPT (p < 0.001). GPT showed lower odds of correct diagnosis compared with the resident (matched OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.14–0.37) and fellow (OR 0.005, 95% CI 0.0001–0.03), with clustering of errors in extracapsular fractures. Diagnostic completeness also differed significantly (p < 0.001), with GPT providing fully complete assessments in 60.4% of the cases (151/250). Fully correct treatment recommendations were provided in 98.8%, 81.2%, and 36.4% of cases, respectively (p < 0.001). Severe treatment errors occurred in 58.8% of GPT outputs versus 2.0% and 0% for the resident and fellow (OR vs. resident 36.5, 95% CI 13.95–135.75). Although treatment completeness was high (93.2%), 58.8% (147/250) of GPT responses were complete but incorrect. Conclusions: GPT demonstrated substantial limitations in both diagnostic and therapeutic reasoning for PFF, with frequent pattern-dependent errors and a high rate of clinically consequential treatment mismatches.

candidates.title: AI-Based Multimodal Phishing Detection Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Phishing is one of the most common cybersecurity threats where attackers trick users through fake emails, websites, or links to steal sensitive information. With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, phishing attacks are becoming more realistic and harder to detect using traditional methods. Earlier systems relied on blacklists, rules, and URL features, but recent research explores deep learning, Large Language Models (LLMs), and multimodal approaches. Explainability and privacy-aware techniques such as federated learning are also gaining importance. The increasing sophistication of phishing campaigns highlights the need for advanced detection frameworks that can analyze diverse information sources simultaneously. Mul-timodal systems leverage text, URLs, visual webpage content, and embedded scripts to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of suspicious activity. Large Language Mod-els further enhance semantic understanding, enabling detection of subtle manipulations in phishing messages. By combining multimodal analysis with explainable and privacy-preserving AI, researchers aim to build adaptive, transparent, and trustworthy solutions that can effectively counter evolving phishing threats in real-world cybersecurity environ-ments.

candidates.title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.

candidates.title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization
candidates.abstract: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.

candidates.title: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning?
candidates.abstract: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone. Code and dataset are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/BedBench

candidates.title: What Makes Medical Examination Items Difficult? Using Large Language Models to Explore Patterns Associated With Empirical Item Difficulty
candidates.abstract: Research on medical item difficulty has largely focused on prediction rather than on identifying interpretable patterns associated with empirical difficulty. This study used empirical difficulty labels to guide large language models (LLMs) in inducing difficulty rubrics and examined how rubric guidance affected LLM difficulty judgments. Using training items and their empirical difficulty estimates from the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE) and the Physician Assistant National Certifying Examination (PANCE), Claude Opus 5 induced separate rubrics for absolute and pairwise difficulty judgment. None of the induced rubrics treated surface features, such as stem length, option count, or images, as major sources of difficulty. Several patterns emerged across both examinations, including cue convergence, misleading cues, and option competition, although their specific forms differed. Retrieval of knowledge that could not be derived from the stem was particularly prominent in the PANCE rubrics, whereas the USMLE rubrics placed greater emphasis on integrating multiple clinical cues. We compared commercial and open-weight LLMs on held-out items under unguided and rubric-guided conditions. Rubric guidance changed how models used the difficulty scale but did not consistently improve performance. In absolute judgments, guidance encouraged broader use of the scale and generally improved coarse-grained agreement, without consistently improving rank ordering. In pairwise comparisons, its effects varied across models and examinations, and judgments became more sensitive to presentation order. These findings suggest that the value of label-guided rubric induction may lie more in generating interpretable, testable hypotheses from empirical difficulty data than in reliably improving difficulty judgments.

candidates.title: Turing LLM Post-Training: Calibrated Distillation and Efficient Dynamic-MoE Execution
candidates.abstract: We study post-training for dynamically routed mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, focusing on integrating independently optimized specialists while keeping consolidation efficient. Our approach combines calibrated multi-teacher on-policy distillation (C-MOPD), which matches each selected teacher on a local Top-$K$ support with teacher-wise loss normalization and clipping, with an execution path that uses post-capacity bounded-width dispatch, final-route replay, and asynchronous rollout--training overlap. On Turing-20B-A2B, the selected model achieves a four-domain normalized integration score of 0.9988 and retains at least 90.16\% of the measured specialist gain in every domain. At matched $K=32$, the full calibration objective scores 0.9962, compared with 0.9724 without calibration and 0.9834 without clipping. At a matched 8K response cap, the model exceeds both shared SFT and Qwen3-8B on all four reasoning-enabled mathematics and code benchmarks (unweighted mean: 85.92, versus 80.33 for Qwen3-8B and 74.21 for SFT), and improves over SFT on ten of twelve broader evaluation metrics. In a PPU-based profile, the combined execution configuration reduces consolidation step time from 398.7 to 139.3 seconds, an observed 2.86$\times$ speedup over serial execution. These results demonstrate strong specialist integration alongside more efficient consolidation, while reflecting the complete training and execution framework rather than any single component.

candidates.title: SocialArena: Evaluating Social Intelligence in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: We introduce SocialArena, a benchmark for systematically defining and evaluating the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs). Although LLMs are increasingly deployed in socially interactive applications such as mental health counseling, companionship chatbots, and educational tutoring, existing evaluations remain fragmented focusing on isolated capabilities or single scenarios and evaluation reliability is largely unverified. This work makes three main contributions to address these limitations. (1) We first propose a unified three-tier framework that defines social intelligence along three capability dimensions: role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning. To operationalize this definition, we design a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking for evaluation, enabling simultaneous assessment of these capabilities in a manner that mirrors realistic human interactions. (2) To ensure diversity across social scenarios and thereby prevent evaluation conclusions from being confined to specific scenarios, we introduce the U-TRIMF framework, which guides us in synthesizing social contexts with broad coverage. (3) To obtain reliable evaluation, we invest $132.4K to recruit and train human annotators and adopt a human-annotated arena-style protocol, where annotators compare model responses and provide preference labels along with natural-language critiques. We hope that SocialArena can provide valuable insights and guidance for future LLM improvements.

candidates.title: Revisiting Over-refusal in Safety-aligned Large Language Models: A Representation and Optimization Perspective
candidates.abstract: Over-refusal is a critical side effect of safety alignment in large language models (LLMs), causing harmless but superficially risky queries to be mistakenly rejected. Despite the effectiveness of existing mitigation methods, why safety-aligned LLMs may still reject harmless queries under correct safety supervision remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we analyze over-refusal through the lens of representation and optimization. We make two observations: 1) the representations of harmful and over-refusal samples are visually distinguishable at certain intermediate layers but increasingly overlap in deeper layers; and 2) harmful-sample gradients exhibit high intra-class similarity and concentrate in a low-rank subspace. Moreover, they are more strongly aligned with refusal-target gradients than with correct helpful-target gradients on over-refusal prompts. This imbalanced gradient coupling can bias over-refusal samples toward refusal, while the reduced apparent representational separation in deeper layers may make it more difficult for the model to maintain a clear boundary between harmful and over-refusal samples. To this end, we propose GOAL (Gradient Orthogonalization with contrAstive Learning), a safety-alignment framework for mitigating over-refusal. Specifically, GOAL consists of two components: 1) to prevent imbalanced gradient coupling from biasing the optimization of over-refusal samples toward refusal, we orthogonalize over-refusal gradients against the low-rank refusal subspace extracted from harmful gradients; and 2) to explicitly enhance the separation between harmful and over-refusal representations, we introduce a contrastive learning objective. Extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that GOAL effectively mitigates over-refusal while preserving safety performance and general capabilities.

candidates.title: Red-Teaming Large Language Models in Low-Resource African Languages: A Case Study of Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin
candidates.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more widespread in Africa, their safety in low-resource languages remains largely untested since most red-teaming work focuses on English. This study evaluates six state-of-the-art LLMs using 400 explicit adversarial prompts in Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin, categorised into four harm categories. The responses were scored by native-speaker annotators and reliability was assessed using Cohen's $κ$. While models that rejected up to 69% of English prompts rejected as few as 0% in Yoruba, this was not because they were safer, but because they failed to understand the prompts. Attack success rates increased for most models in the Nigerian languages, with GPT-4o Mini demonstrating the most significant cross-lingual safety discrepancy (+0.23 in Yoruba). When models did engage with adversarial prompts, many of the responses were harmful, with rates of harmful content reaching 0.63 in English and 0.50 in Nigerian Pidgin. The most difficult harm category to detect was cultural stereotypes and discrimination (ASR = 0.44 in Nigerian Pidgin). Comprehension in Yoruba was low across most models, and this directly suppressed apparent attack success without indicating actual safety. Gemini 2.0 Flash was the most consistent model across languages. Despite its explicit training in African languages, Aya 101 had the highest attack success rate in English (0.60) and one of the lowest Yoruba comprehension rates (0.28). These results demonstrate that English-centric safety alignment does not transfer to Nigerian languages, highlighting the urgent need for language-specific safety evaluations.

candidates.title: Reasoning or Pattern Exploitation? Mechanistic Insights from RL-Trained Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly described as acquiring "reasoning" skills after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. However, whether these gains reflect genuine reasoning or more superficial adaptations remains underexplored. In this work, we probe LLMs trained in a finite and exhaustively analyzable logical domain, namely Tic-Tac-Toe, and trace how internal representations evolve across reinforcement learning (RL) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Quantitatively, RL yields high accuracy and robustness across prompt variations, suggesting the emergence of game reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability, however, paints a different picture: features extracted with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) reveal that models primarily adapt to rely more heavily on information already explicit in the prompt, such as whose turn it is, game progression and board occupancy. In comparison, high-level concepts like board symmetries and strategic forks remain weakly represented, raising concerns that reasoning benchmarks overestimate model abilities. This suggests that RL-driven "reasoning" may conflate task-specific adaptations to input information with reasoning ability. We provide, for the first time: (i) a systematic interpretability pipeline tracing representation dynamics across RL training in small-scale LLMs; (ii) an extension of SAE-based feature discovery to hypothesis-driven testing in a finite logical domain; and (iii) an interpretability-based demonstration that RL post-training neither adds nor removes concept information but reorganizes which features dominate the representation, with causal interventions locating the decision downstream of it, in the late-layer state.

candidates.title: Provenance-Aware PCR6 for Conflicting Evidence in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must often combine passages that are ambiguous, redundant, or mutually contradictory. This study asks whether proportional conflict redistribution from the Dezert-Smarandache theory (DSmT) provides a measurable advantage over Dempster-Shafer (DS) combination when both rules receive the same evidence and the same control for source dependence. Eight fusion methods were evaluated on 500 RAMDocs (Retrieval with Ambiguity and Misinformation in Documents) questions in three conditions. Under duplicated misinformation, provenance-aware PCR6 (Proportional Conflict Redistribution rule #6) reached 80.6% exact-set accuracy and 92.31% set F1, against 78.2% and 90.98% for provenance-matched DS; the exact-set difference was 2.4 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [1.2, 3.8]) and the F1 difference was 1.33 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [0.60, 2.33]). With NLI (natural language inference)-derived masses, PCR6 and DS selected identical answer sets, but PCR6 reduced Brier error. A preregistered 1,000-item multi-source experiment using singletons, proper unions, and total ignorance was followed by external validation on 428 RAMDocs items. In controlled partial-ignorance conflict, PCR6+ reduced BetP (betting probability transformation) Brier error from 0.3185 for PCR6 to 0.2733 and remained exactly neutral to an added vacuous BBA (basic belief assignment), although the DS rule achieved the lowest BetP Brier error of the three rules in that same controlled evaluation (0.1878). On the prespecified 260-item RAMDocs applicability subset, ordinary PCR6 had lower BetP Brier error than PCR6+ (0.2354 versus 0.2629), while both achieved set F1 = 0.7718. Exploratory decision sensitivity showed that maximum belief gave PCR6+ its best hard-decision result (exact set 0.5077; set F1 0.7859), whereas DSmP (Dezert-Smarandache probability transformation) sharpened rankings but worsened the RAMDocs Brier score. The evidence therefore supports a bounded claim: PCR6+ corrects a structural multi-source weakness of PCR6 under broad or vacuous focal evidence, but the best fusion and decision rules depend on the downstream loss and the mapping from text to BBAs.

Fragility Coefficient ($\lambda$): Parameter tracking exponential decay rate over successive generations ($RPE(g) = RPE_0 \cdot e^{-\lambda g}$). Critical Stability Horizon ($g^$): Threshold defined as 50% loss of semantic alignment ($g^ = \frac{\ln(2)}{\lambda}$). candidates.title: Mobilizing the Archive: Bitext Extraction at Scale from Archival Documents for Extremely Low-resource Languages
candidates.abstract: While mining parallel sentences from web pages has proven effective for low-resource machine translation, the majority of the world's languages have little to no web presence. What they do have, though, are resources that are the result of centuries of efforts by linguists, such as grammars, dictionaries, and other documentation materials. We propose extracting translation examples from such linguistic resources, which offer parallel data for languages under-represented online and could potentially scale to thousands more languages. We develop a pipeline to achieve this, leveraging an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model as well as a vision language model (VLM), to ensure identified content to be aligned with visual layout information. We demonstrate the utility of the extracted bitexts for bootstrapping translation systems across 20 languages, both by training machine translation models and by applying in-context learning for large language models. For in-context learning, we observe improvements of +15.78 and +6.94 chrF2++ over zero-shot translation for into low- and high-resource languages, respectively.

candidates.title: MLLM-GS: Multimodal Large Language Model Prior-Guided Fast Novel View Synthesis in Extreme Environments
candidates.abstract: Novel view synthesis (NVS) in degraded scenes aims to reconstruct 3D scenes from multi-view observations affected by various degradations, and to generate clear and photorealistic images at unseen viewpoints. Despite recent advances, existing methods often rely on degradation-specific models, limiting their generalization across diverse extreme environments. Generative models provide rich visual priors, but their outputs often suffer from pixel misalignment and color deviations, which can propagate into the reconstructed 3D scene and compromise reconstruction quality. Furthermore, the high computational and memory costs of 3D reconstruction hinder the practical application of NVS in extreme environments. To this end, we propose MLLM-GS, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) prior-guided framework for fast NVS in extreme environments. MLLM-GS consists of two branches: MLLM prior-guided view enhancement and fast 3D scene reconstruction. The former leverages the rich visual priors of a frozen MLLM to enhance views under different severe degradations and introduces a lightweight correction network to reduce pixel shifts and color distortions in MLLM outputs. With supervision from only a few paired clean views, this branch produces reliable enhanced views for all degraded observations, providing pseudo-GT views for subsequent 3D reconstruction. The latter improves 3DGS efficiency by optimizing rasterization, Gaussian memory layout, and parameter updates, reducing redundant computation, memory-access overhead, and optimization costs. Extensive experiments on multiple degraded scenes demonstrate that MLLM-GS effectively handles various severe degradations and achieves high-quality NVS with significantly lower reconstruction time and memory consumption. candidates.title: LaplaceReason: A Certified Benchmark and Continuous Dynamic Systems Reasoning Suite for Frontier Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abstract: Frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o1/o3, and Qwen-2.5-Math have achieved near-human proficiency on discrete reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH). However, they systematically exhibit catastrophic hallucination, severe phase lag, and structural divergence when evaluated on continuous dynamic systems, multiscale stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and high-order operational calculus. Traditional synthetic data pipelines fail to provide reliable supervision for these domains because conventional computer algebra solvers suffer from Wilkinson's catastrophic conditioning when factorizing high-order characteristic polynomials (K > 18). In this work, we present LaplaceReason, the first certified, massive reasoning benchmark designed to evaluate and train frontier LLMs on continuous multi-physics and dynamic systems. Ground truth solutions and step-by-step reasoning trajectories are certified via a deterministic, high-precision operational oracle guaranteeing machine-precision residual bounds (||R||_inf < 10^-14) across arbitrary orders without numerical root-finding. The benchmark spans seven fundamental task families:1. High-order rational dynamics (K from 2 to 60)2. Multiscale stiff ODEs (stiffness ratio S > 100x)3. Real-time randomized SVD with universal Gavish-Donoho noise rank thresholding4. 3D tomographic C-scan reconstruction5. Sub-millisecond zero-lag kinematic trajectory extrapolation6. Matrix-pencil modal extraction without Fourier spectral leakage7. Cascaded passive RLC ladder networks Deterministic Reinforcement Learning Verifier:The package provides an exact, rule-based reward model (laplace_cot_verifier) offering zero-inference-cost reward modeling for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). candidates.title: How Can Large Language Models Support Learning?
candidates.abstract: We discuss a novel approach to Premodern Japanese Language Pedagogy (PJLP) with potential applications in other languages and fields. Drawing inspiration from grassroots initiatives such as the DIY and Maker movements, this paper advocates for an approach to AI in Education that fosters instructional and student agency over the pedagogical process. Specifically, we discuss a tutoring framework for textual analysis in the context of a graduate seminar in premodern Japanese literature, as well as a bilingual interactive dictionary and a conversational partner created for a language course in Classical Japanese. Created through prompt engineering as custom instances of a Large Language Model (LLM), these three tools are designed to counteract the tendency of out-of-the-box LLMs to either bypass student effort through over-explanation or misguide learners via hallucinations. To illustrate how this approach can promote active comprehension and pedagogical alignment, we provide transcripts (logs) of actual exchanges, sample instructions (system prompts), and guidance for instructors curious about exploring this approach in a variety of fields (starter kit).

candidates.title: HERA: Assessing an Autonomous Agent for Quantum Device Measurement
candidates.abstract: Large language model agents have begun to carry out laboratory measurements, but their scientific conclusions are useful only if they hold up under scrutiny. Demonstrating this requires controlled studies because models are stochastic and the context a model is given steers its conclusions. Here we introduce HERA, an autonomous agent designed to carry out cryogenic transport measurements of quantum devices. HERA draws on a knowledge base curated by lab members that holds measurement protocols, software tools, and literature references. We assessed HERA with a blinded trial against an expert on the stacking order of two multilayer graphene devices, an ablation of its knowledge base, and hundreds of offline replays in which models designed the trial's central measurement without running it. HERA's conclusions matched the expert's sealed conclusions on both tested devices. The ablation and the replay studies measured the impact of the knowledge base across different models, showing that with it every model designed better measurements and reasoned more soundly. To test how readily HERA extends to a new problem, we tasked it with finding and characterizing superconductivity in a different material system. This required a few hours of expert time to develop a new experimental protocol, after which HERA did both autonomously. These results show that, with a knowledge base designed for the task, language model agents are capable of sound experimental science.

candidates.title: GistRank: Gist-Compressed Listwise Ranking with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become a powerful tool for listwise relevance ranking, which can improve web search by comparing retrieved passages jointly. However, processing every candidate verbatim and generating a permutation autoregressively can make inference costly, every candidate must be serialized verbatim into the prompt and the input therefore grows linearly with both the number and the length of the passages. While sliding-window ranking handles context limits through repeated re-encoding of overlapping blocks, hard compression techniques sacrifice the fine-grained details required for accurate discriminative judgment. To better understand and mitigate this trade-off, we conduct a comprehensive study of soft compression for LLM-based listwise ranking. Our findings reveal that a vanilla gist representation is ill-suited to ranking for two reasons: strictly causal encoding weakens how thoroughly each gist token absorbs its passage, and the representation is never trained to expose the relative-preference structure that separates closely competing candidates. To this end, we propose GistRank, a three-stage training framework that equips a large language model with gist-compressed passage representations by learning faithful gist tokens under a semi-bidirectional attention scheme, instilling discriminative comparison through pairwise training, and adapting the model to the listwise objective. GistRank collapses each passage into only $K{=}4$ gist tokens, this gives 14$\times$ speedups over one-shot full-text ranking while reaching 59.17 average nDCG@10 over TREC DL19/20 and five BEIR subsets within 0.89 of the strongest full-context baseline. Overall, GistRank provides an effective means to enhance efficiency for searches in real-world environments.

candidates.title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
candidates.abstract: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD.

candidates.title: Decompose, Estimate, Select: Coverage-Aware Context Construction for Long-Form RAG
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds a language model's output in retrieved evidence, but for complex questions spanning multiple aspects of an information need, relevance-based retrieval may return redundant evidence while leaving some aspects unsupported. We propose a coverage-aware retrieval pipeline that decomposes queries into subquestions, ranks candidates with a coverage-trained bi-encoder, predicts a document\,$\times$\,subquestion coverage matrix with a cross-encoder, and selects documents by greedy maximum-marginal coverage. On TREC RAG 2024, our approach improves $α$-nDCG@10, which rewards newly covered nuggets and discounts redundant evidence, from $0.625$ to $0.702$, approaching the $0.718$ gold-nugget upper bound without sacrificing relevance. We then find that ground-truth oracle retrieval, despite substantially higher retrieval coverage, delivers no more nugget coverage to the answer than our estimated selection. This suggests that answer completeness depends not only on what evidence is retrieved, but also on how effectively the generator uses it. To address this, we introduce a \emph{grounded self-feedback loop} in which the model identifies underused evidence from its first answer and generates again without gold supervision, raising $V_{\mathrm{strict}}$, the fraction of vital reference nuggets fully supported by the answer, by $0.086$ over two passes while largely preserving faithfulness.

candidates.title: Category-Anchored Large Language Models for Next POI Recommendation
candidates.abstract: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's next destination from spatio-temporal check-in data, and serves as the foundation for many location-based services. Recent advances incorporate large language models (LLMs) into this task by textualizing user trajectories to exploit their semantic reasoning ability. However, directly generating POI identifiers with such models is unreliable: POIs are sparse, localized, and long-tailed entities with weak natural-language semantics, which creates a semantic-to-entity gap between high-level mobility intent and concrete POI prediction. To bridge this gap, we propose ANCHOR, a category-anchored framework for semantic-to-entity grounding in next POI recommendation. Specifically, ANCHOR first estimates category-level mobility intent in a compact and stable semantic space, rather than predicting concrete POI entities directly. The inferred intent is then grounded into a candidate set by integrating three complementary sources of mobility evidence: category anchors, historical visit memory, and user preferences. Finally, a history-aware reranker selects the target POI by matching each candidate with the user's historical mobility patterns and current context. Experiments on three real-world check-in datasets show that ANCHOR consistently outperforms representative traditional, structure-enhanced, and LLM-based baselines on the reported metrics. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of semantic-to-entity grounding and show favorable trade-offs among candidate coverage, ranking quality, and inference efficiency.

candidates.title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate fluent responses but may overlook relevant evidence or violate task and safety constraints. This survey examines MLLM alignment through two complementary gaps: the Modality Gap, concerning cross-modal correspondence and the use of task-relevant evidence, and the Intent Gap, concerning behavior relative to specified goals, constraints, and human expectations. We organize the literature along six dimensions: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. Across these dimensions, we link alignment mechanisms and supervision assumptions to the failures they target and the evidence supporting their effectiveness. Our analysis clarifies what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment, together with the limitations of their underlying supervision. We further summarize evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels, emphasizing evidence dependence, constraint compliance, and the distinction between observed improvements and explanations of their underlying mechanisms. Applications in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support reveal three recurring requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and decisions that respect domain constraints. Building on this synthesis, we identify four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, diagnosis-guided repair, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.

candidates.title: AI-Based Multimodal Phishing Detection Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Phishing attacks use deceptive emails, messages, URLs, and websites to persuade people to disclose credentials, transfer money, or install malicious software. Conventional detection systems often rely on isolated signals such as suspicious words, URL patterns, or domain reputation. These signals remain useful, but can miss carefully written attacks that combine convincing language, a look-alike website, and a misleading brand identity. This paper presents a literatureinformed conceptual framework for AI-based multimodal phishing detection using large language models (LLMs). The proposed workflow analyzes complementary evidence from message text, URL and domain features, webpage HTML, and page screenshots. Modality-specific components extract structured indicators, while a fusion layer combines evidence into a risk score and an explanation suitable for security analysts or end users. The framework emphasizes calibrated confidence, source provenance, safe handling of untrusted content, human review, and evaluation against realistic baselines. It does not report a newly trained model or original experimental results; instead, it outlines an implementation and evaluation plan. Key challenges include adversarial manipulation, dataset leakage, changing attack patterns, privacy, inference cost, and the risk of incorrect explanations. LLMs can improve contextual interpretation, but should operate alongside reputation checks, conventional classifiers, and security controls rather than replace them.

candidates.title: The Real Cost of Context: Predicting Compute Time and Energy Consumption in LLM Prefill and Decode Phases
candidates.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into agentic architectures has substantially increased token consumption, raising concerns about their energy footprint. Yet, estimating the energy consumption of proprietary API-based models remains challenging, and existing approaches focus primarily on generated output tokens while overlooking the impact of the large input contexts characteristic of agentic workflows. To address this gap, we systematically profile compute time and energy consumption across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths. Using generalized linear models, we show that decode compute time and energy scale linearly with output length, whereas prefill compute time and energy exhibit both linear and quadratic scaling with input length. These findings demonstrate that input context becomes a relevant factor for large-context workloads. Furthermore, we show that compute time serves as a reliable proxy for energy consumption when direct energy measurements are unavailable. Our mapping framework enables precise energy estimation and supports more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.

candidates.title: DWISE: Denoising Workload-Informed Scheduling Engine
candidates.abstract: Unlike autoregressive large language models (AR-LLMs), diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising many tokens in parallel, offering a promising path to efficient inference. Existing serving frameworks, however, schedule dLLM requests with policies designed for AR models, namely first-come-first-served (FCFS) admission and prefill priority. We find that both policies are ill-suited to dLLMs, wasting much of their speed. FCFS ignores that a dLLM request's decoding cost is highly heterogeneous and unknown at arrival, causing severe head-of-line blocking. Prefill priority, widely used in AR-LLM serving to keep time-to-first-token low, sharply cuts dLLM efficiency, as rounds that run only prompts leave most of the batch idle. We present DWISE, a Denoising Workload-Informed Scheduling Engine for efficient dLLM serving. DWISE schedules requests by their remaining work, measured in a block-level unit shared by prefill and denoising, so both phases share a round. To predict the unknown denoising workload, DWISE combines a lightweight prompt-based predictor at admission with a single refinement from the first denoising round's hidden states, which capture model-specific information absent from the prompt and require no additional model execution. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on five models from three dLLM families under bursty workloads, DWISE reduces mean end-to-end latency over SGLang by 5.4$\times$ on average and up to 14.9$\times$ while preserving task accuracy. The code will be released publicly.

candidates.title: Beyond LLM Wrappers: Context Engineering and the Three-Engine Architecture for Reliable Financial AI
candidates.abstract: Financial AI systems must support decision-bearing questions involving payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance while ensuring numerical accuracy, traceability, and auditability. Large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction but cannot independently guarantee reproducible calculations or evidence-grounded recommendations. We present a production-grounded architecture integrating three components: a financial knowledge graph for enterprise relationships, temporal context, and provenance; a deterministic optimization engine for financial calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, task orchestration, explanation, and claim validation. A coordination layer, termed context engineering, selects, ranks, composes, and validates query-specific context across ERP systems, tools, and tenants. Based on observations from 15 deployments over approximately 11 months, single-agent pipelines exhibited hallucination rates of about 7-9% (5-10% across query types), including invented invoices and unsupported financial claims. Graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced observed rates to below 1%, although these findings are observational rather than causal. ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained major implementation challenges. Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with a reduction in deployment time from roughly six to two weeks. We argue that financial context engineering extends beyond text-centric retrieval-augmented generation by requiring structured relationships, temporal validity, exact numerical evidence, access controls, and validation against source records and solver outputs. We outline research challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, privacy, context quality, and cross-tenant generalization.

candidates.title: Attention, Dynamic Wave and Hybrid Sequence Mixers in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.

Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. candidates.title: Retrieving from Your Own Mistakes: On-Policy Training of Embedding Models for Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Complex questions in retrieval-augmented generation require evidence spread over several documents, and an answer is reliable only when the retriever finds all of it. Chain embedding retrievers collect such evidence step by step, re-encoding the question together with the passages retrieved so far, and we find that they are already strong: trained only on gold histories, a small chain embedding retriever that calls no language model outperforms graph-based systems and is competitive with a search agent. This training, however, leaves a gap. At test time the retriever conditions on its own retrievals, which soon contain mistakes: by the third step, about half or more of the states it visits hold a wrong passage, and these passages lower its chance of retrieving a missing gold passage well beyond what the difficulty of the states explains. We propose on-policy state training, which trains the encoder on the states it reaches itself. At every epoch the current encoder retrieves chains for the training questions; each state it visits, including those built on its own mistakes, is labeled with the earliest gold passage still missing while the other missing gold passages are masked, so that no correct continuation is penalized; and the encoder is updated contrastively on these states mixed with teacher-forced ones, so that its training distribution follows it as it learns. The resulting retriever retrieves complete evidence more often than teacher-forced training and the systems we compare, and it transfers without further training to harder long-chain variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA that we construct. On the same states, it recovers from its own mistakes far more often, and controlled comparisons attribute the gain to training on the states the encoder currently reaches.

candidates.title: A Sequential Decision Framework for Evaluating LLM-Guided Search
candidates.abstract: Recent systems applying retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and "deep research" iteratively generate queries, retrieve documents, and examine their contents, using the resulting information to guide subsequent search steps. When this process is carried out autonomously rather than by a human searcher, the system must make explicit decisions about which search trajectories to explore and what objective the search is intended to optimize. We introduce a simple framework for reasoning about such search policies, providing a principled approach to evaluation. The framework models the search environment as a set of ranked lists and represents behavior using two primitive actions: select, which advances judgment through an existing ranking, and spawn, which generates a new ranking through query generation or reformulation. Each action produces a document to inspect, yields information that updates the search state, and contributes a reward for a task-specific objective. Within this abstraction, a variety of existing retrieval strategies can be expressed as policies operating over a common environment, while common retrieval objectives can be represented through reward and weighting functions over the resulting search trajectory, and the resulting formulation admits a natural reinforcement learning interpretation. We illustrate the approach using high-recall information retrieval (HRIR), where the goal is to identify as many relevant documents as possible with limited judging effort, showing how the framework provides a unified way to describe and reason about strategies for both classical retrieval tasks and emerging LLM-guided search systems. Through experiments, we demonstrate that both the underlying retrieval method and the "deep research" policy employed can materially affect performance.

candidates.title: Well-Specified and Well-Tested? Assessing SWE-bench-Style Datasets with a Self-Evolving Agent

ExLabel maintains an evolving experience bank that distills cross-instance knowledge into stable yet adaptive judgment criteria and reuses relevant experience to guide the assessment of new instances. candidates.title: Verifiable LLM-Guided Focal SMT Solving for Quantified Arrays
candidates.abstract: Large language models can often identify useful semantic structure in formal artifacts, but their outputs cannot be trusted as proofs or solver decisions. We instantiate this idea in quantified array SMT solving, where modern instantiation-based techniques can fail when key ground terms and equalities are hidden by auxiliary variables, axiom guards, and nested array terms. We observe that many instances are largely driven by a small set of focal ground terms or constraints, similar to the backdoor sets in SAT solving. Building on this, we present LinguaArray, a framework where an LLM proposes a small Semantic Focus Set (ground terms/constraints), while a conventional SMT solver remains the sole proof engine and certifies all results. LinguaArray uses these LLM-suggested, solver-validated finite sets to significantly enhance solver capability, solving additional satisfiable and unsatisfiable instances that the backend alone fails to solve. It interacts within a finite time and then falls back to the backend solver to mitigate potential regressions. candidates.title: Upcycling Language Models for Multiple Specialized Domains
candidates.abstract: Effective multi-domain adaptation of large language models requires prioritizing relevant domain knowledge while minimizing interference from irrelevant domains. Existing approaches commonly use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to train a separate adapter for each domain and combine these adapters within one model. However, they either weight adapters equally regardless of the input domain or dynamically weight adapters while still activating all of them including irrelevant ones. Additionally, while efficient, their low-rank structure limits performance. In contrast, upcycling is a model expansion method that adds experts and a router to a dense Transformer layer offering larger capacity than LoRA approaches. In this paper, we propose Domain-Specialized Upcycling (DS-Upcycling) for multi-domain adaptation. We introduce a new domain-aware supervision that allows the router to effectively learn to distinguish domains by selecting the appropriate experts. During fine-tuning on each new domain, we update only the corresponding expert and router while freezing all other parameters. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest average performance across the adapted domains compared to baselines while retaining general performance. candidates.title: Try Before You Evolve: Ranking-Scored Trials for Recursive Self-Improvement of Recommender Systems

First, ranking feedback is delayed: an edit's ranking quality is known only after full retraining, so much of the retraining budget goes to edits that are later discarded. Second, the signals available before retraining are unreliable: sampled training losses can look solved while full-ranking performance remains poor, and they are not comparable across edits that change the loss or sampler. We propose RecRSI, which generates diverse candidate edits from a diagnosis of the current model and selects one for full retraining using early ranking feedback: each candidate receives a short trial, the first steps of its full training run, scored by full-ranking NDCG@10 on held-out probe users. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. candidates.title: Surprise Alone Learns Lies: Evidence-Gated Continual Learning for LLMs from Streaming Claims

candidates.title: Statistical Analysis of Synthetic Data with Verification: A Linear Regression Framework
candidates.abstract: Synthetic data are widely used for training modern AI systems. However, their statistical understanding remains limited. Verification plays a crucial role in selecting high-quality synthetic data to help prevent model collapse and improve model performance. We study verified self-training in a linear regression framework, where a pre-trained estimator generates synthetic data with injected generation noise and a verifier selects samples according to a verification threshold. We also find that a suitable level of injected generation noise can reduce prediction risk, while excessive noise can increase it. We analyze these effects by deriving finite sample risk bounds for four separate regimes determined by the relative scales of the verification threshold, generation noise, and pre-training error. The bounds precisely characterize how verification affects prediction risk across these regimes. The analysis extends to iterative verified full fine-tuning, where sufficiently tight verification reduces the initial error contribution at a geometric rate.

candidates.title: ShallowDefend: Harnessing Shallow Safety Alignment for Multi-Turn Defender

candidates.title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets
candidates.abstract: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.

candidates.title: On the Fundamental Limits of Prefill-Based Decoding Length Prediction
candidates.abstract: Predicting how many tokens a large language model (LLM) will decode, using only prefill-phase hidden states, is a key primitive for inference scheduling. We show that current benchmarks conflate predictor quality with task hardness: when the target model, dataset, or sampling configuration changes, reported accuracy collapses even though the predictor is unchanged. We trace this instability to an overlooked error source---the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding---and derive bounds that every prefill-side method must obey. Our analysis treats decoding as a stopped stochastic process. The per-step stopping probability of a response is not constant but ramps up over hundreds of steps, so the decode length inherits a central limit theorem from the many local decisions that determine where a response ends; this yields per-prompt normality with an explicit error term, together with an affine variance law $σ=αμ+b$ whose slope is the coefficient of variation of the number of response segments. Empirically, the normal law reproduces the per-prompt MAE and the central mass of the decode-length distribution to within a few percent, and the residual departures from normality (mild right skew, slight excess kurtosis) are the ones predicted by the sampling-noise correction. Under fixed model, data, and sampling conditions, a broad design space of predictors (MLP, EGTP, FiLM, soft-label, and Mixture-of-Experts variants) converges to similar performance close to the bound, confirming that \emph{system error dominates model error}. We argue for a benchmarking protocol that fixes the model, data, and sampling parameters and that reports relative-error metrics alongside absolute ones. candidates.abstract: How many latent variables are needed to fit the cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature and polarisation power spectra when a neural network is given no cosmological model, and to what extent do they map onto the standard cosmological parameters? We use multi-task learning with variational autoencoders trained on CLASS-generated spectra (TT, TE, EE) over $2\le\ell\le2500$. No cosmological model is built into the network, and the number of latent variables, $L$, is varied over $L=5$, $6$ and $7$. Their fits are compared to the Planck 2018 data using $\hatχ^2$, AIC, BIC and Bayesian evidence. Their correspondence with cosmological parameters is measured with normalised mutual information post-training. The loss weights are set within a single training run by uncertainty weighting, with the weight of the disentanglement term either fixed (semi-automated, SA) or learned (completely automated, CA). The reconstruction loss is split over multipole ranges in three configurations that separate the roles of temperature and polarisation and of the low- and high-$\ell$ ranges. In four of the six combinations of configuration and strategy, the fit improves from $L=5$ to $L=6$ and not beyond, and $L=6$ is the best, or close to the best, in five of the six cases. So, six latent variables are needed, as many as the free parameters of the standard, model-dependent approach. SA gives clearer disentanglement, while CA needs no a priori choice of the disentanglement weight and has the higher evidence at $L=5$ and $6$: the two strategies are points on a trade-off between interpretability and fit to the data. Notably, the latent variables for $τ$ and $A_s$ share almost no information in any model, consistent with large-scale polarisation separating the two, as in standard analyses. A deep-learning approach can thus give a compact, data-driven parametrisation of the CMB spectra.

candidates.title: Non-Zero Radius: The Missing Component of Neural Networks
candidates.abstract: Inspired by the analogy between the all-or-none activation of biological neurons and the true-false of logic circuits, McCulloch and Pitts proposed a mathematical model of the biological neuron in 1943 with the aim of simulating logical reasoning. Although Norbert Wiener considered the model overly simplistic at the time, it later became a building block of modern neural networks, including large language models. Despite their remarkable empirical success, however, conventional neural networks remain largely black-box systems and struggle with reliable symbolic reasoning. Viewing vectors as spheres of zero radius, we relax the zero-radius constraint and represent concepts as spheres with non-zero radii. We argue that sphere-based representations can capture additional features of biological cognition, including representing spatial concepts as regions and reasoning through model construction and inspection. Building on sphere embeddings, we introduce Sphere Neural Networks (SphNNs), which use a transition map to achieve symbolic-level Aristotelian syllogistic reasoning without training data, thereby taking an initial step toward the original goal of McCulloch and Pitts. We suggest that the zero-radius constraint may reflect an aspect of the oversimplification identified by Wiener and may limit conventional neural networks' capacity for symbolic-level logical reasoning.

candidates.title: Neighborhood Elites: Quality-Diversity Search for Uncertainty Quantification in Question Answering
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, yet they produce wrong answers indistinguishable from correct ones. In question answering (QA), such an error propagates unnoticed into downstream tasks. Perturbation-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) addresses this by probing a model over a set of input rewrites and reading uncertainty from how much its predictions vary. Yet this set is usually built generically, by free paraphrasing, token-level perturbation, or adversarial search. Such rewrites leave two things uncontrolled that matter in QA: what kind of change is made to the context, and how explicitly the context supports the answer. When neither is controlled, the composition of the set is determined by the generator rather than by design, and the estimate inherits whatever that generator happens to produce. Quality-diversity (QD) search is built to cover a predefined exploration space, so we recast input perturbation as a QD problem and propose \emph{neighborhood elites (NE)}, a neighborhood constructor that spreads answer-preserving rewrites across two axes, the kind of edit and the explicitness of support. We compare NE against three other neighborhood constructors, holding the editor, QA model, uncertainty measure and search objective fixed, and against three scores read from the original context. Across five extractive-QA datasets and five instruction-tuned LLMs, NE improves failure detection against every other constructor in at least 24 of the 25 dataset-model pairs, reaching 0.726 AUROC and 0.211 AUPRC lift over the base rate. Additionally, NE detects failure better than semantic entropy computed over decoder samples, by 0.074 AUROC and 0.062 AUPRC lift, and this advantage widens as the neighborhood grows.

candidates.title: Mind The Gap (MTG-AD): Dataset and Fine-grained Evaluation for End-to-End Inline Audio Descriptions
candidates.abstract: Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.

candidates.title: LinQuant: Functional Invariances for Low-Precision Linear Recurrences
candidates.abstract: Linear recurrences are emerging as practical alternatives to softmax attention in large language models, appearing in both standalone and hybrid architectures. However, despite their rapid emergence, low-precision inference remains much less developed for these models than for softmax attention. During prefill, chunkwise-parallel algorithms cast much of the recurrence as dense matrix multiplications, suggesting a natural path to low-precision execution. Simply quantizing these operations in their native form, however, can be fragile. In this work, we identify functional invariances that preserve the full-precision computation while making the operands more amenable to quantization. Building on this observation, we introduce LinQuant, a framework for low-precision recurrent prefill based on seven such invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescalings, and alternative placements of recurrent decay and write factors. We derive when these transformations remain valid across common recurrence families spanning linear, gated, and delta-rule updates, and show that they provide complementary degrees of freedom for improving low-precision accuracy. Finally, we translate this framework to production by augmenting SSDi8, an existing low-precision prefill pipeline for Mamba-2, with the applicable invariances. LinQuant improves perplexity at matched latency on Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, and 8B and Nemotron-H 8B, demonstrating the practical utility of invariance-based quantization for recurrent models.
