candidates.title: Compiling Autoregressive LLM Control into Policy-Exact Parallel Inference for Hierarchical RAG
candidates.abstract: Large language models increasingly act as controllers in structured decision pipelines, yet their decisions are still executed by autoregressive text decoding. Hierarchical RAG is one such setting: at each frontier of a document tree, an LLM commits to $b$ of $k$ sections under an input-dependent action grammar, executed as either failure-prone free-form JSON or reliable but strictly serial grammar-constrained generation. We show that this serialization is unnecessary for bounded-horizon control: the reachable future forms a shallow action-prefix tree, which we compile --- one root prefill plus one tree-causal probe evaluate every prefix-conditioned action distribution with serial decoding's tokens, positions, and causal ancestry. A prefix-state lemma makes compiled control policy-exact in exact arithmetic: the same policy with a two-forward critical path and zero output tokens. One further probe pass certifies the exact order-marginalized MAP set. Across four document-disjoint splits and two scales on the primary MetaX device, compiled control matches the serial policy on $84$--$89\%$ of questions --- every instrumented divergence a floating-point near-tie --- and cuts control latency by $35$--$47\%$ versus token-wise serial decoding and $6$--$7\%$ versus an idealized chunked engine; an H800 repetition preserves the ordering.

candidates.title: TRIAD: Benchmarking Omni-Modal Ambiguity in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Ambiguity is a central feature of natural communication: a sentence, image, or sound may remain underspecified until evidence from the other channels is considered. Yet current multimodal benchmarks mostly test perception, recognition, or reasoning over already determinate inputs, leaving unclear whether omni-modal large language models can resolve ambiguity distributed across text, vision, and audio. We introduce TRIAD, a benchmark for omni-modal ambiguity resolution. Each item is a text--image--audio triplet paired with a question and a set of answer options, and is constructed so that the full triplet determines a unique answer while removing any one modality makes the set of consistent options non-unique. TRIAD contains $327$ hand-written queries in $86$ scene groups and covers $18$ ambiguity categories across the three modalities. Evaluating $14$ omni-modal systems reveals that strong item-level performance does not translate into robust scene-level disambiguation: the best model still trails humans by over $20$ points in group accuracy. Removing answer options widens the gap further, driving model group accuracy to the single digits while humans remain robust. Leave-one-out and transcript/description counterfactuals further show that current systems often underuse audio cues when text and image are present. TRIAD reframes omni-modal evaluation around disambiguation rather than recognition, and provides a taxonomy, benchmark, and diagnostic protocol for measuring this capability.

candidates.title: Segmentation-Aware and Context-Reranked Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Vietnamese Question Answering
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances knowledge-intensive question answering by integrating document retrieval with neural generation. The framework is evaluated on the ViQuAD2 and ViHealthQA benchmarks using 10 independent runs with different random seeds. Experimental results show that SADR improves first-stage retrieval robustness, while CoRe provides substantial additional gains through contextual reranking. Their integration in SADR-CoRe-Gen achieves highly competitive performance, with best or tied-best results on several evaluation metrics across the two benchmark datasets. candidates.title: Secure Multi-Agent Collaboration Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: As Large Language Models have emerged and become increasingly significant, the way to develop smart multi-agent systems has been transformed, enabling them to communicate, collaborate and decision more efficiently. These systems rely on agents working independently which need to effectively and safely coordinate their actions, to maintain reliability in messy realworld environments. However, bringing LLMs into the mix introduces new risks like data leaks, trickery from bad actors, and trust issues. This paper breaks down a full plan for keeping multi-agent teamwork secure when using LLMs. We look at everything from how they are built and the rules they use to communicate to the safety tools used to stop attacks. We also talk about where this is being used now, the hurdles we still face, and where the tech is headed for building secure AI ecosystems

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Urdu Islamic Jurisprudence: A Review of Design Choices and a Reference Architecture
candidates.abstract: Questions about Islamic law need exact answers with sources. A wrong citation is a serious failure. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fits this need, but Urdu is a low-resource language and there is little guidance for building such a system. This paper reviews the design choices behind an Urdu Fatawa RAG system and proposes a reference architecture. We compare Urdu-capable language models, embedding models, tokenizer cost, vector databases, primary data stores, and backend frameworks against four requirements: faithfulness to sources, precision on close jurisprudential terms, Urdu fluency, and private self-hosting. We argue for chunk-level storage of question-answer pairs, hybrid dense and sparse retrieval fused by reciprocal rank fusion, a prompt with English instructions and an Urdu output example, and a three-container deployment that separates inference, vector search, and the API. Our choices rest on published benchmarks, not on a controlled comparison on our own corpus, and some remain hypotheses. We state which ones, and we give an evaluation plan.

candidates.title: Predicting Music Valence and Arousal via Textual and Multimodal In-Context Learning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: While arousal can be reliably predicted from musical audio, emotional valence remains difficult to model due to its subjective and context-dependent nature. In this work, we investigate the potential of in-context learning (ICL) with large language models to advance continuous valence and arousal prediction. Rather than predicting emotion scores directly, our framework leverages contextual demonstrations from an auxiliary dataset to refine the initial predictions produced by a small, task-specific base model. We systematically evaluate a text-based ICL variant using lyrics and generated audio captions, alongside a multimodal variant that incorporates raw audio signals. Using the entire MER60 dataset strictly as a held-out test set, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains, particularly for valence. Text-based ICL improves the valence $R^2$ from 0.110 to 0.427 with 80 demonstration shots, while the multimodal variant achieves 0.346 with only 10 shots. These findings suggest that training-free ICL offers an effective inference-time strategy for current language models to predict continuous music emotion.

candidates.title: Large language models for multimodal clinical predictive modeling: a systematic review
candidates.abstract: The electronic health record (EHR) comprises structured and unstructured data, both of which are integral for comprehensively representing patient history. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has enabled the incorporation of unstructured data modalities into machine learning models that leverage EHR data. In this systematic review, we characterize studies that utilize LLM-enabled multimodal predictive modeling with EHR data. Following a screening of 641 studies, 57 met inclusion criteria. We identified three strategies for LLM-based multimodal integration: embedding, extraction, and text fusion. Delineated by the format of the unstructured data at the time of fusion, all strategies yielded performance gains (average 6.4% increase) over single modality models. LLMs facilitated modeling by generating note-embeddings for downstream prediction, extracting clinically informative variables, and summarizing long text documents prior to integration. Building on our review, we identified LLM-enhanced predictive modeling considerations that include sample size, interpretability, and computational costs. This study supports the potential value of LLMs for EHR-based predictive modeling and provides a framework for future multimodal modeling tools.

candidates.title: Harnessing Language Models as Optimization Modeling Agents
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language optimization problems into solver programs, but reliably producing correct formulations and implementations remains challenging. Existing approaches improve optimization modeling through agentic workflows or task-specific post-training. This raises a practical question: can a lightweight harness using a single model role achieve competitive performance without additional training? We introduce OPTICYCLE and OPTISTATE, two lightweight inference harnesses for optimization modeling, and evaluate them on nine benchmarks comprising 2,634 problems using 11 Qwen variants spanning 0.6B-27B parameters. Our results show that execution-guided revision consistently improves macro accuracy over direct generation for all evaluated models, with gains of up to 49.46 percentage points. Despite their simplicity, both harnesses outperform six adapted agentic workflows in same-model comparisons and four evaluated post-trained optimization models at comparable model sizes, without additional training. Explicit formulation state provides further but model-dependent improvements, suggesting that additional structure is not universally beneficial.

candidates.title: Grammar of Presence: Language, the Subject, and the Large Language Model
candidates.abstract: Grammar of Presence is a philosophical monograph built on a single thesis: language is not the property of the human. It has always been a machine for producing reality, and with large language models (LLMs) that machine appears in its pure form, as a system that speaks without having an "I". The book asks what happens to education, to the subject, and to encounter once language no longer guarantees the human. The argument unfolds in three steps. - Ontological (Chapters 1–2). Language is treated as production rather than reflection. The book draws on Wittgenstein (meaning as use, the language-game and form of life), Latour (language as a network), and Fazi (contingent computation), then turns to Bourdieu, Foucault, and the algorithm as a new type of power. Format is treated as an ontological category.- Pedagogical (Chapter 3). If language is produced without a subject, what do we teach, and how? This step offers a typology of subjecthood in education, the LLM as a participant in learning, and a "pedagogy of the gap".- Existential (Chapters 4–6). This step examines subjecthood after the death of the subject: the actant, Rousse's criteria and two registers, and the levels of consciousness C0, C1 and C2. It then turns to contingency and becoming and to the encounter between human and machine, read through Levinas, fear and trust, and the fideism of meaning. The book is written partly as a dialogue between two voices, KZ and DV, so it enacts the encounter it describes. It closes with a (non-)conclusion. Appendix A gives the specification of the Third Protocol v1.2, a formal grammar for human–LLM dialogue: signal format, codes, states, intents, admissibility conditions, transition rules, and sample dialogues.

candidates.title: Disagreement reliability routing for multimodal large language model evidence pipelines with imperfect counterfactual priors
candidates.abstract: Abstract Multimodal large-language-model (LLM) evidence pipelines often attach rule-derived outcomes to candidate remediation actions even though only the executed action yields a factual production outcome. Treating those counterfactual rules as ground truth can miscalibrate routing, while discarding them wastes structured operational knowledge. We introduce EviRoute-DR, a disagreement-reliability routing method that learns when rule priors fail and combines corrected-rule experts with direct factual outcome experts through a reliability-conditioned meta-learner. The study uses 2,100 production cases, seven candidate actions per case (14,700 case-action records), and exactly one observed production outcome per case. Base models are trained on 600 factual cases, combined on 200, and evaluated on 1,300 held-out factual cases spanning main, temporal-labelled, hard, and workflow-shift cohorts. On factual outcomes, EviRoute-DR achieves AUC 0.926 and Brier score 0.0910, compared with 0.921/0.0971 for direct logistic regression and 0.924/0.0922 for a random-forest baseline. The paired bootstrap Brier improvement over logistic regression is 0.0060 (95\% CI 0.0021--0.0092). A separate production-derived counterfactual replay shows a stronger cost-resolution frontier at moderate operating costs, reaching approximately 0.815 resolution near 12 cost units. Because the logged action is always the argmax of the production score vector, we do not interpret those scores as stochastic propensities and make no inverse-propensity, doubly robust causal, or production-effect claim. The results support disagreement-aware reliability fusion as a practical methodology for evidence routing under partial factual feedback.

candidates.title: CONTEXT OVER LANGUAGE: PERSONA-DRIVEN INTERTEMPORAL CHOICE IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as experimental subjects in behavioral and economic research. However, it remains unclear whether their decisions reflect stable preferences or context-dependent responses. This study examines intertemporal choice behavior in LLMs within a controlled experimental framework. We implement a fully factorial design across four models (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Claude), varying persona (financially stressed vs. disciplined), delay (1 vs. 6 months), reward magnitude (650–900 $), and prompt framing (direct vs. human-like). Each condition is repeated to approximate response distributions. Results show that LLM behavior is structured but not preference-stable. Decisions are primarily driven by persona conditioning: financially disciplined agents choose delayed rewards significantly more often than stressed agents. Delay and reward magnitude affect choices in line with temporal discounting, while prompt framing has negligible effects. We interpret these findings by conceptualizing LLMs as context-dependent behavioral simulators rather than agents with stable preferences. The contribution is not to establish human equivalence, but to identify the internal consistency and structure of LLM responses under controlled variation. Overall, the results highlight the importance of experimental design and suggest that LLM outputs should be understood as conditional simulations rather than stable expressions of preference.

candidates.title: Autoregressive Multimodal Anomaly Detection with Large Language Models for Microservice Systems
candidates.abstract: Microservice systems have become a dominant architecture for large-scale cloud applications, enabling rapid deployment and elastic scaling. However, ensuring the reliability and availability of microservice systems critically relies on effective anomaly detection, as failures and performance anomalies can quickly propagate across services and severely impact end-to-end system behavior. Existing multimodal anomaly detection approaches for microservice systems often struggle with two fundamental limitations: (i) the neglect of modality-specific characteristics in favor of cross-modality fusion, and (ii) the "identity-shortcut" problem that affects the feature reconstruction process. To address these issues, we propose LLMMAD, an autoregressive multimodal anomaly detection framework for microservice systems based on Large Language Models (LLMs). Initially, to reconcile cross-modality fusion with modality-specific preservation, LLMMAD embeds and recombines multimodal data into a unified sequence for LLM processing to model inter-modality relationships, while employing modality-wise reconstruction heads to retain modality-specific information. Subsequently, to eliminate the identity-shortcut, we implement a prediction-driven autoregressive objective, under which the model predicts future states rather than copies current inputs. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on three real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that LLMMAD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving F1-score improvements of 3.1%, 1.4%, and 0.9%, respectively, thereby providing a more reliable solution for microservice monitoring.

candidates.title: A Visual Grounding Benchmark for Retinal OCT with Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer clinical questions about medical images, but trustworthy use requires visual grounding: models should localize the pathology they report rather than rely on spurious shortcuts. Whether MLLMs can visually ground clinical findings in retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT), the most widely used imaging modality in ophthalmology, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RetinaGroundBench, the first benchmark for biomarker visual grounding in retinal OCT. It comprises 815 B-scans exhaustively annotated by ophthalmologists with 4,537 bounding boxes covering 13 biomarkers across 8 diseases. Because MLLMs often fragment a single lesion into multiple partial predictions, we propose AggIoU, a metric that evaluates whether the union of overlapping predicted boxes covers the annotated region. Across 27 open-source MLLMs (0.8-38B parameters), we find that visual grounding remains largely unsolved: the best general-purpose model achieves a macro F1 of just 23.7%, with consistently low recall, despite reaching up to 73% balanced accuracy on biomarker presence questions. To narrow this gap, we developed RetGrounder, an MLLM fine-tuned using an OCT-specific strategy integrating grounding and textual information. Despite its relatively small size (8B), RetGrounder improves grounding F1 to 33.9%, a 43% relative improvement. Our benchmark provides a reference point for measuring progress in the field of OCT diagnosis with MLLMs.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Taxpayer Advisory in an LMIC Setting: A Proof-of-Concept Evaluation of Statutory Legal Retrieval
candidates.abstract: Abstract Objective Tax administrations in low- and middle-income country settings are expanding digital services, yet reliable, legally grounded taxpayer guidance remains difficult to scale. This study developed and evaluated a proof-of-concept retrieval-augmented generation framework for taxpayer advisory using national income-tax legislation as an authoritative knowledge source. The objective was to test whether semantic retrieval could identify statutory provisions accurately enough to support grounded downstream language-model prompting. The legislation was transformed into 198 knowledge units, embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, indexed in ChromaDB, and evaluated using 900 automatically generated questions linked to expected provisions. Results The retriever achieved 72.00% Top-1 accuracy, 86.78% Top-3 accuracy, 28.93% Precision@3, 86.78% Recall@3, and mean reciprocal rank 0.7880. Many Top-1 errors were recovered within the first three results, indicating ranking ambiguity among semantically related provisions rather than complete retrieval failure. The prototype integrated legal document processing, vector search, provision retrieval and structured prompt construction in an end-to-end workflow. The results support technical feasibility for grounded taxpayer information, but generation quality, legal correctness, usability and compliance effects were not evaluated. Validation should include additional tax instruments, real taxpayer queries, professional legal review, multilingual support and cross-jurisdiction testing before deployment in resource-constrained public-service settings.

candidates.title: Evaluating the Applicability of LLM Inference Optimizations on Apple Silicon
candidates.abstract: Apple Silicon is among the most widely used platforms for local LLM inference, yet nearly all inference optimizations are designed and validated on server-class NVIDIA GPUs under batched serving workloads. Which optimizations retain their benefits when moved to Apple Silicon, and what determines their applicability? We evaluate four optimization families: KV-cache pruning, speculative decoding, ported GPU kernels, and post-training quantization. Experiments span four Apple machines under a common single-request decode workload, with matched RTX 4090 comparisons where possible. KV-cache pruning can reach up to 1.75 times end-to-end throughput on Apple but can reduce throughput on desktop NVIDIA GPUs. Under the common benchmark, all evaluated speculative decoding methods reduce throughput on Apple, despite reported 2-6 times gains on server GPUs. CUDA kernel designs transfer only partially: public Metal lacks asynchronous copy, and batch-one decode makes several serving-oriented mechanisms inapplicable, although transferable components yield up to 1.20 times decode throughput. Quantization gains vary by machine. Across four families, a reported speedup is not a portable property of a technique alone but a joint function of technique, runtime, hardware contract, and workload regime.

candidates.title: Amplifying Latency and Cost of LLM Inference via Rowhammer Attack
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high inference efficiency using optimized GPU kernels generated by just-in-time (JIT) compilation frameworks such as Triton. Triton compiles GPU kernels through an MLIR/LLVM-based pipeline. We investigate whether a Rowhammer-induced bit-flip in the CPU's DRAM can degrade GPU-based LLM inference performance while preserving output correctness. We present LLVMhammer, the first Rowhammer attack that causes LLM inference slowdown by inducing a bit-flip in Triton's compilation pipeline. A bit-flip in a performance-critical optimization pass causes Triton to generate a functionally identical but suboptimal GPU kernel. Since Triton caches the generated kernel on disk, a single successful bit-flip causes persistent slowdown across subsequent inference executions. Triton's target-independent stages are shared across GPU vendors, which makes our attack GPU vendor-agnostic. To identify exploitable bit-flip locations without manual inspection, we build Karnage, a tool that isolates useful bit-flip locations in Triton's target-independent compilation pipeline. We evaluate LLVMHammer across a diverse set of LLMs, including Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Deepseek-llm-7B-chat, across NVIDIA RTX 4090 and AMD RX 7900 XTX GPUs. LLVMhammer increases inference latency of an LLM inference server running on a single GPU by 4-16\%, which, in turn, can translate into additional annual operating costs at the scale of multi-GPU deployments. We further show that LLVMhammer can also corrupt LLM outputs across different GPU vendors, reducing BERTScore to as low as 25\%, illustrating the broader security implications of bit-flips in Triton's compilation pipeline.

candidates.title: Steering Black-Box Large Language Model Agents with Pitfall Anticipation World Model
candidates.abstract: Frontier black-box Large Language Model (LLM) agents are proficient at long-horizon reasoning and precise action generation. However, when it comes to a specific agentic task, they have no internalized knowledge of how that particular environment unfolds. A world model offers a natural remedy, providing the agent with environment specific knowledge by foreseeing how the environment will respond to the action it is about to take. Prior world models for LLM agents mainly predict next observations at each step, which is costly and often uninformative because individual observations provide limited task-relevant guidance and not every step requires call for foresight. This raises a key question: what a world model should predict and when should it be invoked for agentic tasks? Our pilot study suggests that world model guidance is most useful when it anticipates pitfalls within a bounded multi-step future. Motivated by this, we introduce Pitfall Anticipation World Model (PAWM), which selectively intervenes when a potential pitfall arises and predicts the impending failure to steer the agent away from it. PAWM is trained in two stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on synthetic data labeled with agent pitfalls, followed by GRPO co-training with a black-box LLM to further optimize it in the target environment. PAWM improves Claude Sonnet 4.5 performance by 24.3% on ScienceWorld and 7.7% on WebArena-Lite, outperforming a range of baselines. These results demonstrate that PAWM provides an effective form of world model guidance for black-box LLM agents.

candidates.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality
candidates.abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds large language models in external knowledge. Modern pipelines combine embedding, chunking, retrieval, reranking, query augmentation, context compression, and agentic verification, yet these techniques are typically evaluated one at a time. It remains unclear whether their isolated gains survive composition, whether retrieval quality and answer faithfulness favor the same design choices, and whether conclusions from small corpora hold at large scale. We pre-declare three hypotheses and introduce LASAGNA, an open-source framework for controlled RAG evaluation. We test 450 configurations across eight benchmarks and corpora ranging from 5K to 200K documents. Three findings emerge. First, individually strong techniques from different phases of a RAG pipeline do not necessarily compose: three retrieval techniques predict a +47% combined improvement but deliver only +17% when used together. Second, component gains stack differently for retrieval and faithfulness, and optimizing one can hurt the other. Third, the best composition changes as the corpus grows: the combination that wins on a small corpus may not remain best at large scale. These findings show that gains measured in isolation are not reliable predictors of realistic performance, and that new RAG techniques should be tested with the full surrounding stack. We call on researchers to do so and supply LASAGNA to simplify these experiments.

candidates.title: Newly Important Is Not Newly Built: What Reasoning Post-Training Adds Inside a Language Model, Why the Evidence Separates Representation From Wiring From Deployment, and the Cross-Model Tests That Would Show an Attention Head Is New
candidates.abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Reasoning models are built by post-training a pretrained model with supervised fine-tuning on teacher traces, with reinforcement learning against a verifier, or with both, and a running dispute asks whether this builds new machinery or redirects machinery the base model already had. A 2025 circuit study gave the first side a concrete form: attention heads that are absent from the base model's reasoning circuit and present after post-training, many of them after distillation and supervised fine-tuning, fewer and less stable after reinforcement learning. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that "new" has at least three separable meanings inside a model - a new representation, new wiring that consumes a representation, and a new policy for when existing behaviour is deployed - and that the measurements now in the record each speak to one of them. A head that enters a thresholded attribution circuit is newly important; whether it is newly built is a further question that the comparison as run cannot answer, because the reference model differs from the distilled model's actual parent, the circuit is defined by contrasting the two models' own response styles, and zero-ablation effects in the same study do not separate emergent heads from base-circuit heads or from heads taken from an unrelated task. The strongest cross-model evidence points to a regime split at the level of deployment: base-model steering vectors directed by the thinking model's own gating recover about 76% of the accuracy gap for reinforcement-learned models and about 11% for distilled ones, and a gap-matched pair computed from that study's table preserves the split. At the level of representation, a direction taken from the base model drives backtracking in a distilled model but not in the base. The paper consolidates these values in two tables and a figure, gives a classification procedure, and names five cross-model tests that would show whether a post-training head is new.

candidates.title: MAPS: Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning for Regulating Search Momentum in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by retrieving external knowledge. Recently, some RAG methods interleave reasoning and retrieval, enabling LLMs to progressively generate sub-queries and retrieve external knowledge. However, these methods may suffer from redundant or ineffective sub-queries and insufficiently diverse query exploration. Moreover, due to the tightly interleaved nature of reasoning and retrieval, it remains unclear how the evolving reasoning process influences query intent. To characterize the evolution of query intent during reasoning, we introduce search momentum, which captures the accumulated retrieval tendency induced by historical changes in generated sub-queries along the reasoning trajectory. Through momentum-based analysis, we find that the query generation process tends to continuously evolve along existing retrieval trajectories. Based on this observation, we propose MAPS, a Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning framework for regulating search momentum and mitigating query-intent drift. MAPS first retains the retrieved knowledge and a refined reasoning state, thereby reducing the influence of historical reasoning trajectories on subsequent sub-query generation. Subsequently, MAPS extends the conventional sequential reasoning process into a parallel reasoning paradigm. At each iteration, MAPS identifies complementary retrieval directions, generates corresponding sub-queries for parallel retrieval, and consolidates the retrieved evidence to update the knowledge and reasoning states. Experiments on six question-answering benchmarks demonstrate that MAPS consistently outperforms representative RAG methods across different backbone models. All code and resources are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/MAPS.

candidates.title: Omnilingual-MsASR: Benchmarking Multimodal, Multilingual, Long-Form Multi-Speaker ASR of Omni Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio and video understanding. However, existing models struggle with long-form, multi-speaker videos, especially in understanding the entire video and recognizing who says what and when. To characterize the capability limit of current omni LLMs and guide future model development, we introduce Omnilingual-MsASR, a multilingual, multimodal benchmark for long-form Multi-speaker Automatic Speech Recognition (MsASR) covering six languages, recordings up to 30 minutes, and scenarios with up to 20 speakers. Omnilingual-MsASR provides parallel audio and video inputs to evaluate models' cross-modal consistency and their ability to exploit complementary cues across modalities. Extensive evaluations of leading omni-modal LLMs reveal substantial performance bottlenecks, while their tcpWERs frequently exceed 100%. These findings highlight fine-grained temporal localization, speaker disambiguation, and cross-modal synergy as key challenges for future omni-modal foundation models. Our work is available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-MSpeaker.

candidates.title: C$^2$U in RAG: Compositional Concept Unlearning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation can expose unwanted concepts through retrieved evidence even when the generator is moderated. We study query-side concept suppression with a fixed encoder and document index. Compositional Concept Unlearning (C$^2$U) routes a profile-derived direction through an augmented atom bank, adding only a bounded edited-minus-original delta to the raw query. Across five datasets, four encoders, and three seeds, the validation-selected configuration reduces pooled binary target Hit@5 by 4.25 percentage points with non-positive control degradation and target-exposure changes. Under the evaluated query transforms, it suppresses target density without increasing budgeted control-query exposure. Separately, ArXiv four-concept composition improves over an averaged-direction comparator after independent validation gates and first-use test evaluation.

candidates.title: NPUGen: NPU as KV Generator for Stable Long-Context Mobile LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: As on-device large language model (LLM) applications like mobile agents become increasingly popular, long-context inference has become a key challenge. The key-value (KV) cache is the foundation of efficient autoregressive decoding, but its memory footprint grows rapidly with context length, often exceeding the memory limits of mobile devices. Existing KV cache management methods, such as compression and storage offloading, often lead to performance degradation or unpredictable stall latency. We find that in the prevalent CPU/GPU-decoding mobile pipelines, the NPU remains largely idle during decoding and can recompute missing KV cache more efficiently than storage offloading. We therefore propose NPUGen, whose KV recomputation engine generates missing KV cache on the idle NPU via a prefill-like forward pass, avoiding unstable storage I/O, CPU intervention, and unnecessary data movement. NPUGen further introduces a hidden-state anchor mechanism that eliminates redundant prefix recomputation, and turns KV recomputation into a schedulable background service to cope with resource contention and guarantee foreground QoS. Experiments on smartphones with Qualcomm SoCs across multiple long-context tasks show that NPUGen significantly reduces decoding latency and fluctuations, providing fast and stable long-context inference on resource-constrained mobile devices.

candidates.title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long-context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short-context tasks. Therefore, we propose $\textbf{LongZero}$, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long-context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi-document context. LongZero combines these self-written multi-hop reasoning tasks with self-written multi-round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long-context reasoning of LLMs.

candidates.title: SimPT: An Automated Simulation Framework for Intervention-Based VLA Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Human-in-the-loop (HIL) post-training improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies through expert corrections, but costly human supervision and repeated real-robot evaluation limit algorithm exploration and development. We introduce SimPT (Simulation-based Post-Training), a simulation framework that automates intervention-based VLA post-training by integrating policy rollouts, corrective data collection, policy training, and standalone evaluation. To automatically determine intervention timing and recovery strategies, we develop an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph that tracks task progress using privileged simulator state and retains stable snapshots during policy execution. After a rollout fails, a CuRobo-based expert attempts recovery from these snapshots, starting at more advanced task stages and falling back to earlier ones as needed to generate corrective trajectories. We implement and compare four post-training methods, RECAP, HG-DAgger, DPO+SFT, and FlowPRO, across seven RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Relative to a fixed-interval snapshot baseline, the Progress Graph reduces recovery attempts by 75.0% and increases recovery success from 93.4% to 98.9%. Using SimPT, we develop RECAP-CF-LPF, a refinement of RECAP that combines cross-fitting and low-pass filtering of value predictions. This refinement increases the overall success rate from 76.50% to 79.36% in held-out simulation trials. In real-robot HIL post-training, it increases the success rate from 72% to 96% across 25 scenarios of an Ethernet cable-insertion task. These results demonstrate the utility of SimPT for exploring and developing VLA post-training algorithms.

candidates.title: Post-Training Weight Quantization in Small Language Models: Reasoning–Efficiency Trade-offs Across GGUF Precision Levels
candidates.abstract: Weight quantization can reduce the storage and computational requirements of languagemodels, but it may also affect their reasoning capabilities. This study investigates whetherquantization causes gradual or abrupt degradation in the reasoning performance of smalllanguage models. Three instruction-tuned models were evaluated: Qwen3-0.6B, Gemma 3 1BIT, Llama 3.2 1B Instruct. Each model was tested using a BF16 reference version and fiveGGUF quantization formats: Q8_0, Q6_K, Q5_K_M, Q4_K_M and Q3_K_M.Evaluation was performed on the same fixed 50-question subset of the GSM8K mathematicalreasoning dataset. Exact-answer accuracy, average latency, peak RAM usage, generationspeed, and stored model size were recorded. The results show that quantization did notproduce one universal degradation pattern. Accuracy changes varied across models andprecision levels. Qwen Q4_K_M matched its BF16 accuracy, Gemma Q4_K_M recorded a numerically higher accuracy than BF16 in this pilot sample, 44% versus 42%; this small difference should not beinterpreted as evidence of a meaningful improvement, and Llama Q6_K achieved the highest quantized accuracy for that model. However, Q3_K_M produced larger accuracy reductions for Qwen and Llama.Quantization consistently improved storage and inference efficiency. These findings suggestthat quantization provides practical efficiency benefits, but the effect on reasoningperformance is model-dependent.Keywords: weight quantization; small language models; GGUF; reasoning; llama.cpp;inference efficiency, GSM8K

candidates.title: Parallel Thinking for Large Language Model with Path Diversity
candidates.abstract: Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by exploring multiple reasoning paths simultaneously. However, we identify that parallel thinking via Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically suffers from the mode collapse of reasoning paths, where parallel thinking trajectories degenerate into similar ones. This homogeneity undermines the fundamental motivation of parallel thinking, that is, maintaining multiple hypotheses concurrently to prevent premature loss into a suboptimal solution. In this paper, we propose Diverse Parallel Thinking (DPT), a simple yet effective RL approach for parallel thinking designed to encourage path diversity. DPT rewards the model to develop distinct reasoning strategies by penalizing the prefix similarity of parallel thinking paths, thereby enhancing a more comprehensive exploration of the reasoning space. We conduct various experiments and analyses across multiple reasoning benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of DPT. Results show that DPT successfully outperforms previous parallel thinking methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance over baselines. We validate path diversity as a key element to improve parallel thinking. Our code is available at https://github.com/JiaruQian/DPT.

candidates.title: Multimodal artificial intelligence and large language models in gastrointestinal endoscopy: From lesion detection to workflow-integrated report generation
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, with most early applications focusing on computer-aided detection and diagnosis of lesions from endoscopic images.However, real-world endoscopic practice extends beyond image interpretation.Endoscopists must integrate real-time video, anatomical location, lesion morphology, procedural context, histopathological findings, clinical history, and standardized terminology to make diagnostic decisions and generate clinically meaningful reports.Recent advances in multimodal AI and large language models (LLMs) provide an opportunity to move beyond isolated endoscopic image analysis toward more comprehensive endoscopic workflow support.By integrating visual, textual, temporal, and clinical information, these models can support lesion characterization, anatomical navigation, procedure quality assessment, structured documentation, report generation, and patient-centered communication.Nevertheless, clinical translation remains limited by scarce high-quality multimodal datasets, heterogeneous reporting standards, insufficient external validation, hallucination risk, limited interpretability, real-time integration challenges, privacy concerns, and evolving regulation.This review summarizes current applications of AI in GI endoscopy, with particular emphasis on the emerging role of multimodal learning and LLMs in bridging lesion detection, context-aware interpretation, and automated report generation.Furthermore, the article analyzes future challenges and the methodological, clinical, ethical, and regulatory requirements for the reliable integration of these systems into clinical endoscopic practice.

candidates.title: Experimental reasoning in large language models
candidates.abstract: Abstract Scientific reasoning requires interaction with the physical world: designing experiments, interpreting outcomes, and deciding what experiment should come next. Here we show that general-purpose large language models (LLMs) already possess substantial capabilities for experimental reasoning. We connected LLMs to a liquid-handling robot and camera through PEARL, which provides perception, action, and persistent state. Given objectives rather than prescribed workflows, the system designed and successfully executed experiments, interpreted observations, and revised its approach as evidence accumulated. When information was insufficient, PEARL autonomously designed and performed intermediate experiments to acquire it. In quantitative enzyme characterization, it judged whether measurements were sufficient, new data were required, or conditions needed to change. Across eight scenarios, these behaviors were reliable with limited agent scaffolding and no supplied scenario-specific recovery recipes. More broadly, general-purpose LLMs may provide a reasoning layer between scientific objectives and physical experimentation, shifting laboratory automation from executing predefined procedures toward AI systems that participate directly in the experimental process.

candidates.title: Emotional Framing and Decision Shifts in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in everyday decision-making, concerns about cognitive biases extend beyond human judgment to the systems designed to support it. Large Language Models (LLMs) are frequently consulted for advice across various domains, often treated by users as impartial and expert advisors. This reliance is particularly pronounced in sensitive contexts, such as mental health support and personal counseling, where individuals increasingly turn to AI as a virtual advisor or sounding board for delicate life choices. However, little is known about how these models process emotionally charged information or whether they maintain objectivity when confronted with affective distress. The primary purpose of this study is to investigate whether LLMs exhibit an "affect heuristic" similar to that of human decision-makers, by systematically assessing how emotional framing influences risk evaluation and decision-making recommendations independently of objective statistical facts. To operationalize this, the study evaluates models across four distinct life scenarios (Professional, Interpersonal, Clinical, and Financial), where models are prompted to assess risk on a scale and provide a categorical recommendation (Accept vs. Reject the option). To quantify framing distortions, we introduce the LLMs Emotional Elasticity (LEE) index, a novel metric designed to measure the impact of affective framing on LLMs' risk perception relative to objective probabilities. Using a balanced factorial design combining these scenarios, emotional frames (neutral, negative, and positive), and leading LLM architectures, we evaluate systematic response policies to understand how affective context influences algorithmic judgment. Expected Outcomes: We expect to find that LLMs do not rely solely on objective probabilities, but instead exhibit measurable sensitivity to emotional framing. Specifically, we anticipate that negative frames will consistently elicit higher risk scores and trigger loss-averse decision shifts (driving recommendations toward rejection), whereas positive and neutral frames will yield more balanced evaluations. Furthermore, we expect to demonstrate that emotional elasticity and decision shifts vary significantly across different model architectures and decision domains, identifying which systems are more resilient to affective bias. Ultimately, this research aims to establish the LEE index as a scalable and reliable tool for auditing algorithmic reliability and cognitive stability in AI-based decision support, highlighting critical implications for safety in mental health and personal guidance applications.

candidates.title: AI-Based Multimodal Phishing Detection Using Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Title: AI-Based Multimodal Phishing Detection Using Large Language Models Description: Phishing attacks are becoming increasingly sophisticated, making traditional detection techniques less effective against evolving cyber threats. This research proposes an AI-based multimodal phishing detection framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to analyze email content, URLs, and webpage-related features for identifying potential phishing attempts. The proposed framework aims to combine semantic understanding, URL analysis, and multimodal feature fusion to improve phishing detection, interpretability, and robustness. This paper reviews existing phishing detection techniques, identifies research gaps, and presents a conceptual architecture and evaluation methodology for future implementation and testing. candidates.title: Think-Capture: Active 3D Geometry Acquisition for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at 2D recognition but often fail to maintain consistent 3D relations across sparse viewpoints, leading to spatial hallucinations under occlusion and perspective changes. Existing methods commonly fuse all frames with dense geometry, incurring substantial computation and context overhead while encouraging blind reliance on imperfect estimators. We present Think-Capture, a query-conditioned framework that first identifies task-critical objects and then acquires their geometry on demand. A 3D toolkit lifts zero-shot masks into a common coordinate frame, and a Symbolic 3D State Abstraction compresses object and camera states into structured text. Hierarchical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains the VLM on cases in which geometry either helps or misleads, teaching it when to use tool evidence and when to fall back on visual cues. Think-Capture-4B reaches 54.4% on MindCube-Tiny (+21.5 points over its backbone), 39.1% on the MMSI-Bench positional subset (+7.9), and 42.8% on ViewSpatial (+5.2). It also remains robust under coordinate and mask perturbations. The full stack fits one 24 GB GPU and serves as an asynchronous high-level reasoner on an Agibot G1. Our code is available at https://github.com/819346675/Think-Capture.

candidates.title: Attention Sinks at Long Context: One Log-N Law for Retrieval and Abstention
candidates.abstract: Softmax attention cannot abstain on its own: its weights sum to one, so a head with nothing relevant to read must still attend somewhere. Trained models improvise such a place, the attention sink. Practice now builds one in: a null, an option that absorbs attention and delivers nothing, such as a learned sink logit, a register with zero value or an output gate. We show that these nulls are one mechanism, a gate on an ordinary softmax, and ask what happens to them as the context grows. The answer is one dilution law for two abilities. To retrieve, a matching key must outweigh the N other keys; to abstain when nothing matches, the null must. With bounded scores both leads must grow like log N, and because a query with a match and one without share the same null, no rule that sums over the keys keeps both at long context: a fixed null loses abstention, and a null that grows with the length loses retrieval. Tempering, which scales every score, the null included, by log N / log N_train, provably keeps both under margin conditions, and a head that decides by its largest score escapes the law. Trained heads in a controlled pilot follow the law closely, and tempering keeps both sides there, though not in every harder setting. In 125M-parameter language models, every rule with a null removed the first-token sink and most massive activations; past the training length, keeping positions in range mattered more than the null rule, and adding tempering to YaRN, which already includes a temperature, hurt. In small vision transformers trained at one resolution, tempering at evaluation raised accuracy at higher resolutions. A prespecified test on gpt-oss was inconclusive. This is a working draft, not a final version. It is unpolished in places, incomplete in others, and keeps exploratory material a polished paper would leave out, because that material helps decide what comes next and shows the programme's big picture more fully. Please read it with that in mind: the work will be refined further, and later versions will appear under this record. It belongs to a collection released together on Zenodo: the entry paper The Transformer Abides, the monograph A Spectral Theory of Token Communication, and the papers Attention Sinks at Long Context, The Transformer as a Constrained Equilibrium and Beyond Transformers. This version is the text; the records, the code and the formal proofs follow in a later version.

candidates.title: RISK-KV: Quality-Aware Selective KV Cache Reconstruction for Distributed LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Request migration and interruption recovery in distributed large language model (LLM) inference rely on historical key-value (KV) caches. Retaining or transferring a complete cache incurs substantial state overhead, whereas replaying historical tokens requires additional computation. This paper proposes RISK-KV, a quality-aware method for selective historical KV reconstruction in pretrained models. RISK-KV uses exact KV states on both sides of a target layer and cross-layer ridge regression to predict the missing layer's attention-projection input; it then folds in the original model's KV projection matrices to reduce predictor storage. Reconstruction risk is measured by the change in negative log-likelihood (NLL) caused by actual reconstruction, and low-overhead topology search with quality gating selects the layer groups to reconstruct. Independent tests on three language models show that representative recovery configurations omit 18.2 percent to 33.3 percent of historical KV, with perplexity changes below 0.5 percent. In a local request-recovery experiment with a 512-token history, RISK-KV achieves a 1.51 to 3.31 times speedup over full Token Replay. These results indicate that selective KV reconstruction can reduce historical cache overhead with small changes in predictive quality and improve request-recovery efficiency under the evaluated deployment conditions.

candidates.title: Prism : Efficient Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning for On-Device LLMs
candidates.abstract: On-device fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) is becoming increasingly important for personalized AI assistants and adaptive agents. However, standard backpropagation imposes substantial training-state memory overheads that often exceed the stringent resource budgets of mobile platforms. To address this, Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization leverages forward-only probing instead of backpropagation, drastically reducing memory footprints and offering a compelling alternative for on-device adaptation. Nonetheless, scaling ZO fine-tuning to billion-scale trainable parameter spaces remains challenging, as the cost of recovering reliable update directions scales poorly with dimensionality under mobile constraints. In this paper, we present Prism, a mobile-native infrastructure for practical billion-scale on-device ZO fine-tuning. Prism re-architects the ZO loop around a scalable probing substrate, bringing both per-step training latency and memory overhead closer to the inference footprint. We implement Prism end to end on commodity smartphones and evaluate it across diverse tasks and multiple model scales. Prism achieves accuracy comparable to that of state-of-the-art ZO fine-tuning baselines while reducing per-step latency by 53.4%-76.3% and peak memory by 10.6%-13.8% relative to the best baseline in each setting. These results demonstrate the practical feasibility of billion-scale on-device ZO fine-tuning for LLMs under real mobile constraints. We will release our code to support future research.

candidates.title: Human Oversight for LLM-Assisted Clinical Documentation
candidates.abstract: Clinical documentation is essential to healthcare delivery but is timeconsuming, cognitively demanding, and prone to error. Large language models (LLMs) can generate draft notes, but may introduce hallucinations, unsupported inferences, or factual distortions that clinicians overlook. This study evaluated whether transparency features improve clinician oversight in LLM-assisted documentation. Using a crossover design, 40 clinicians reviewed AI-generated notes under three conditions: a standard LLM interface, token-level uncertainty highlighting, and uncertainty highlighting combined with direct links to electronic medical record fields. Outcomes included factual errors remaining in finalized notes, editing time, trust, perceived control, and cognitive load. The combined uncertainty-plus-source-link interface performed best, reducing factual errors by 41% and editing time by 18% compared with the standard condition. Uncertainty highlighting alone offered partial benefits but still required manual record verification. These findings indicate that LLM-assisted documentation is safer and more efficient when transparency features support verification, direct attention, and preserve clinician control.

candidates.title: HAWK: Heterogeneity-Aware KV Cache Transfer for Efficient GPU-NPU Phase-Disaggregated LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference exhibits distinct computational characteristics across its two phases: prefill is compute-intensive, whereas decode is more memory-bound. As a result, AI accelerators achieve varying levels of efficiency across the two phases. GPUs are well suited to prefill, but are often underutilized during decode. By contrast, NPUs can utilize their compute resources more effectively during decode. Motivated by this observation, we explore a heterogeneous architecture that integrates GPUs and NPUs, mapping prefill to GPUs and decode to NPUs to achieve high performance and efficiency. However, realizing such heterogeneous integration is challenging because LLM phase disaggregation requires KV cache transfer from prefill to decode (that is, from GPUs to NPUs), which is complicated by differences in inter-device communication mechanisms and KV cache tensor layouts. To address this, we propose HAWK, a transfer mechanism that enables rapid KV cache transfer across heterogeneous devices. HAWK establishes a remote direct memory access (RDMA) path for direct cross-device transfers while handling inter-device tensor layout discrepancies as part of the transfer process. In particular, HAWK allocates tensor-layout-aware RDMA buffers on the NPU side to match the target tensor layout. Leveraging these buffers, HAWK orchestrates data transfer from a conventional contiguous GPU RDMA buffer to the corresponding NPU buffers, allowing transferred tensors to be consumed directly without additional data rearrangement while maintaining transfer efficiency. We implement and evaluate HAWK on a system built with commercially available GPUs and NPUs, demonstrating performance within 7.88% of a GPU-only system under the same SLO constraints while achieving up to 1.26$\times$ higher power efficiency and 1.72$\times$ higher cost efficiency.

candidates.title: From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied across the scientific discovery pipeline, from synthesizing literature to generating hypotheses to informing experimental design. A unifying principle behind these tasks is the need to continuously update beliefs as evidence accumulates, for which Bayesian inference provides a natural framework. However, existing work assumes that LLMs cannot carry out principled Bayesian belief updating in context, instead relying on simplifications and heuristics. To challenge this assumption, we present a principled evaluation of Bayesian reasoning capabilities in LLMs, analyzing both the model's internal consistency as well as its ability to recover an externally determined posterior. Specifically, we build an evaluation framework spanning qualitative epistemological examples to probe probabilistic coherence, quantitative benchmarks of Bayesian inference capabilities, and analyses of the impact of non-Bayesian updates on downstream task performance. Across different scenarios, we find that LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule when updating their beliefs in context. However, when equipped with modern reasoning abilities and code execution capabilities, their performance drastically improves, enabling even the close approximation of analytically intractable posteriors. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs with access to appropriate tools could already be used to make complex belief updates in scientific discovery, enabling rapid acceleration of the efficiency and scale of AI-powered scientific discovery.

candidates.title: Networked trust-game data for "Does social networking agency shape trust and reciprocity similarly in large language model agents and humans?"
candidates.abstract: This dataset supports the manuscript “Does social networking agency shape trust and reciprocity similarly in large language model agents and humans?” The archive contains recorded decisions and generated responses from large language model (LLM) agents in a networked trust game, together with executed allocation tables, prompts, synthetic personas and archived experiment configurations. The main experiments comprise three sessions for each of five nominal proportions of free agents (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1). Each session includes 49 agents on a periodic 7 × 7 lattice with four neighbours and lasts 20 rounds. Each agent acts as both trustor and trustee in each round. Free trustors may differentiate investments across neighbours, whereas constrained trustors allocate equally. The three CSV exports contain 14,700 agent-round records in total. A separate exploratory dataset contains one 20-round session per nominal proportion. These sessions used a different instruction concerning terminal-round assumptions and should not be pooled with the main experiments as repetitions of the same protocol. The included README provides the directory structure, experimental conditions, JSON schema, CSV data dictionary and guidance for reuse. Behavioural analyses of the main experiments should use the executed allocations rather than assume that allocations stated in generated text were executed unchanged. Amounts and payoffs are expressed in experimental tokens, not currency. Human benchmark data are not included. They originate from Jia et al. (2025), “Social networking agency and prosociality are inextricably linked in economic games” (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-025-02289-0), and are available from the original authors’ project at https://osf.io/n84dv/. candidates.title: HalluciGuard-eye: knowledge graph-enhanced retrieval-augmented generation for hallucination detection and mitigation in ophthalmic multimodal large language models
candidates.abstract: Background Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of preventable blindness in working-age adults, yet scalable early detection is limited by the unreliability of AI-assisted screening. Multimodal large language models can interpret fundus photographs and support DR grading, but they frequently hallucinate - fabricating lesions or misclassifying referable DR - which directly threatens timely treatment and prevention of vision loss. We developed HalluciGuard-Eye to make AI-assisted DR assessment trustworthy. Methods HalluciGuard-Eye combines knowledge graph-enhanced retrieval-augmented generation with hierarchical hallucination detection. An Ophthalmic Clinical Knowledge Graph containing 47,832 medical entities and 156,294 semantic relationships was constructed from clinical guidelines and published literature. A dual-stream architecture uses a Visual-Semantic Alignment Module to verify cross-modal consistency and a Clinical Factuality Grounding Network to anchor generated content to reranked evidence. The Hierarchical Factuality Score assesses anatomical, pathological, and clinical-recommendation accuracy. The framework was evaluated on four public ophthalmic imaging benchmarks. Results HalluciGuard-Eye reduced hallucination rates by 42.2% compared with state-of-the-art medical multimodal large language models and achieved 91.6% factual accuracy for clinical entity recognition on EyePACS. For diabetic retinopathy grading, sensitivity was 89.6% and specificity was 92.1%, representing improvements of 2.4% and 2.7%, respectively, over MedRAG. In the component ablation, removing knowledge-graph retrieval lowered EyePACS HFS by 9.4 percentage points. Additional analyses yielded 87.6% critical-evidence recall@20, 89.2% lesion-location accuracy, and 88.9% sensitivity in a patient-clustered cohort. Conclusions These results indicate that knowledge-grounded retrieval and hierarchical factuality assessment can reduce hallucinations while preserving diagnostic performance in ophthalmic multimodal language models.

candidates.title: Estimating Decision Rules from Large Language Model Agents: An Application to Bank Balance-Sheet Management
candidates.abstract: Abstract This paper examines whether decisions generated by large language model (LLM) agents can be represented by simple equations in an agent-based model of bank balance-sheet management. In a monthly leader–follower model, a stylised, predominantly deposit-funded euro-area bank chooses deposit rates, lending margins and the composition of bond reinvestment, while depositors and borrowers respond to these decisions and to economic conditions. The initial balance sheet is calibrated to selected indicators from regulatory disclosures. We estimate equation-based approximations of LLM-generated decisions and evaluate them against simulations not used in estimation. Across ten out-of-sample bank-year simulations, the final specification reproduces annual return on equity (ROE) within 0.31 percentage points and meets all fit criteria in seven; none of the deposit-run scenarios meets all criteria. In eighteen simulations with a second LLM family, the ROE difference does not exceed 0.71 percentage points, but only six meet all criteria. Against a market-pricing rule, the original optimisation model, and regression and nearest-neighbour approximations estimated on the same data, the final specification meets all criteria in more years and tracks liquidity most closely in deposit-run years. Instructions without behavioural guidance show that withdrawal magnitudes and fixed-rate borrowers’ price sensitivity depend materially on the instructions supplied; with customer equations estimated under neutral instructions, a two-month withdrawal episode no longer becomes self-sustaining. The results demonstrate a procedure for approximating and evaluating LLM-generated decisions within a defined simulation environment; they do not establish that these responses represent the behaviour of bank managers or customers. candidates.title: Comparative Analysis of Transformer Models for Prompt Injection Detection in Autonomous Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Prompt injection attacks pose a significant security challenge for large language model systems, particularly autonomous large language model-based agents that may interact with external tools, application programming interfaces, and data sources.This study presents a comparative evaluation of five pre-trained transformer models, namely BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, DistilBERT, and ALBERT, fine-tuned for binary prompt injection classification.A balanced dataset of 4,224 samples was compiled from 10 publicly accessible corpora containing benign and injection prompts and divided into training (2,956), validation (634), and test (634) sets.The models were trained in the Kaggle environment using an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, the AdamW optimizer, and a linear warm-up scheduling strategy.On the held-out test set, RoBERTa achieved the highest classification performance, with 97.48% accuracy, 97.52% macro-precision, 97.48% macro-recall, 97.48% macro-F1-score, and 99.64% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.DistilBERT achieved the highest reported throughput of 819.13 samples/s and the lowest per-sample latency of 1.22 ms.Statistical analysis using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and SHapley Additive exPlanations-based interpretability analysis were also conducted to examine model differences and influential linguistic features.The findings demonstrate that fine-tuned transformer classifiers can achieve strong performance on the evaluated benchmark dataset while exhibiting different accuracyefficiency characteristics.However, the results should be interpreted within the scope of the evaluated data distribution, as the study does not include independent external datasets or adaptive adversarial attacks.These limitations indicate that further validation is required to establish generalizability and robustness in real-world prompt-injection defense scenarios.

candidates.title: Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over Federated Cloud Data Lakes
candidates.abstract: Abstract: Enterprise deployments of large language models require grounding generated answers in authoritative, continuously updated internal repositories while strictly enforcing row- and document-level access control lists (ACLs). Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines that chunk PDF documents into fixed 500-token windows and execute unconstrained approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) vector searches fail in production across three dimensions: they lose cross-section structural context in complex financial and technical tables, they suffer lexical blindness on exact product codes and regulatory statutes, and they leak unauthorized knowledge when ACL filtering is applied post-retrieval. This paper presents a federated Enterprise RAG architecture spanning cloud data lakes (Apache Iceberg on AWS S3, Snowflake, and Google BigQuery). Building on foundational RAG formulations (Lewis et al., 2020), ColBERT late-interaction retrieval (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020), and GraphRAG hierarchical community indexing (Edge et al., 2024), our architecture combines layout-aware semantic chunking, contextual header injection, three-way hybrid retrieval (dense HNSW vectors + BM25s sparse lexical + entity knowledge graph traversal) fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al., 2009), cross-encoder reranking, and cryptographic pre-retrieval ACL bitmap filtering. We evaluate the architecture through a production case study modeled on Morgan Stanley Wealth Management knowledge assistants and Ramp automated financial document analysis pipelines over a 14.8-million-document federated corpus. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that hybrid ACL-aware RAG increases Context Recall@10 from 61.2% (dense-only baseline) to 93.4%, raises RAGAS Faithfulness from 0.74 to 0.96, reduces hallucinated ungrounded claims from 14.8% to 1.2%, and enforces zero unauthorized document leakage at a P95 end-to-end retrieval latency of 168 milliseconds. Research Domain & Specialization Track Master of Science in Information Technology (MSIT) — Information Retrieval, Enterprise Generative AI, and Cloud Data Lakes. Core Technical Highlights Empirical Production Case Studies: Rigorous architectural blueprints and telemetry evaluation across enterprise cloud deployments. Four-Tier Reference Architecture: Formal specification from edge ingress to distributed hardware execution pools. Mathematical Formulation: Formally derived algorithmic and optimization models with closed-loop verification. Multi-Modal Benchmarking: Comparative empirical baselines under fault-injection and synthetic workload scaling. candidates.title: A Zero-Shot Multimodal Agent Framework for Power Line Inspection via Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: With the widespread deployment of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in smart grids, visual inspection based on deep learning has significantly advanced. However, conventional object detection paradigms heavily rely on massive, high-quality annotated datasets, struggling with poor generalization and a fundamental “data-hungry” dilemma caused by the extreme scarcity of long-tail defect samples. To overcome these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel zero-shot multimodal agent framework driven by large language models (LLMs). Adopting a centralized star topology, the architecture strictly decouples physical visual perception from high-level business cognition, utilizing an LLM as the cognitive hub and a vision-language model (VLM) as the perception tool. Crucially, the system introduces a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanism to dynamically align visual findings with authoritative grid regulations, supporting rule-referenced report generation. Experimental results demonstrate that, without any domain-specific fine-tuning, the proposed framework reduces false alarms under the tested configuration, with a detection F1 score of 82.52%. In a common-report comparison repeated three times, the framework achieves 65.30% correct reference-clause coverage, compared with 43.84% for a direct Qwen-VL-Max call supplied with the same visual priors and rules. The framework extends visual detection to structured, human-readable reports linked to supplied industrial rules; its grading accuracy and repeatability remain dependent on the visual observations and subsequent tool execution.

candidates.title: Sistem Tanya Jawab Resep Nusantara Berbasis Qwen dan Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Pengembangan sistem question answering pada domain resep masakan menghadapi tantangan dalam menghasilkan jawaban yang koheren secara bahasa sekaligus konsisten terhadap bahan, langkah memasak, dan konteks prosedural dokumen sumber. Large Language Model (LLM) seperti Qwen memiliki kemampuan memahami dan menghasilkan teks, namun berpotensi menghasilkan hallucination ketika jawaban tidak didukung informasi relevan. Penelitian ini mengembangkan sistem tanya jawab resep masakan Nusantara berbasis Qwen dan Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) untuk meningkatkan relevansi dan groundedness jawaban terhadap knowledge base resep. Dataset yang digunakan berasal dari Indonesian Food Recipes Dataset, diproses melalui tahap preprocessing, pembentukan data question-answer, fine-tuning model, dan pembangunan sistem retrieval berbasis vector database. Evaluasi dilakukan menggunakan metrik ROUGE, Recall@K, Grounded ROUGE, Grounded Ingredient Coverage, Answered Rate, dan No-answer Rate. Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan bahwa integrasi RAG meningkatkan kualitas dan keterikatan jawaban dibandingkan model tanpa retrieval, dengan performa terbaik diperoleh oleh skenario RAG + Fine-tuned Qwen yang mencapai ROUGE-L sebesar 0.413, Grounded ROUGE-L sebesar 0.926, dan Grounded Ingredient Coverage sebesar 0.967. Mekanisme tambahan yang dikonfigurasi pada sistem, yaitu no-answer filtering dan fallback retrieval, juga membantu menjaga konsistensi jawaban ketika konteks retrieval yang diperoleh kurang relevan. Penelitian ini diharapkan dapat menjadi langkah awal dalam pengembangan sistem question answering domain-spesifik berbasis LLM yang lebih konsisten dan grounded, khususnya pada pengetahuan prosedural seperti resep masakan Nusantara.

candidates.title: Projected-Feature Scale Calibration for 2-Bit Vision Encoders in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Very low-bit quantization of a multimodal large language model’s vision encoder can impair text recognition and chart understanding. We present projected-feature scale calibration (PSC), an image-only post-training method for 2-bit vision encoders. PSC starts from range-searched GPTQ, fixes integer codes and zero points, and jointly updates existing group scales by matching features through a frozen multimodal projector. This objective aligns image-only calibration with the visual representation supplied to the language model. The learned updates fold directly into the original scales, preserving the inference architecture. Experiments on LLaVA-OneVision show consistent improvements in text recognition and chart understanding over the same strong quantized initialization, including under simultaneous language-model compression. Matched controls support projected-feature supervision over encoder-output reconstruction, repeated calibration samples confirm stable gains, and an unchanged-recipe contrastive language–image pre-training (CLIP) evaluation supports transfer to a second encoder. PSC thus improves the accuracy of compact vision encoders while preserving their quantized representation.

candidates.title: Building a Nested LADDER for LLM Unstructured Post-Training Pruning
candidates.abstract: Non-uniform allocation can improve post-training pruning of large language models, yet quality can still degrade sharply at high sparsity. To control degradation as sparsity increases, we introduce LADDER (Layer-Wise Allocation via Damage-Driven Evaluation and Refinement), which allocates sparsity incrementally. At each step, it evaluates pruning an additional fraction of weights from each eligible layer and commits the layer update that causes the least end-to-end degradation per removed parameter. This process produces non-uniform sparsity profiles and exactly nested masks across multiple budgets. We evaluate LADDER on five OPT, Llama, and Qwen models across 10-90% sparsity, using SparseGPT as its candidate-generation backend and comparing against uniform and adaptive allocation baselines. Results reveal a clear operating-regime trade-off: LADDER is comparable or slightly weaker at benign sparsity but becomes substantially more robust from 70% onward. This high-sparsity advantage largely persists after posterior distillation across four of five models and translates into improved retention of aggregate zero-shot accuracy.

candidates.title: Adaptive Stopping of Streamed Reasoning for Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Reasoning-enabled language model agents can incur substantial computation before acting, although the reasoning needed varies across decisions. Existing stopping signals, such as confidence and intermediate-answer stability, can vary in effectiveness across reasoning models; signals obtained from hidden states or token probabilities also require internal access that may be unavailable or impractical. We introduce StreamStop, which learns model-specific stopping policies offline from prefix-level action agreement. A frozen prefix reader encodes available reasoning text for a lightweight stop head, allowing stopping without access to the reasoning model's internal signals. We construct and publicly release a dataset of agent reasoning trajectories with prefix-level action annotations. These annotations compare each prefix action with the full-reasoning reference action, enabling offline comparison of stopping rules and exact expected-return optimization of a discounted action-agreement objective. Conditioning the head on the discount factor allows the agreement-token trade-off to be adjusted at inference without retraining. In closed-loop evaluations on WebShop and ScienceWorld, StreamStop achieves higher observed success than most validation-selected fixed-budget settings while using fewer reasoning tokens than Full thinking. On WebShop with Qwen3.8-27B, it uses 42% fewer reasoning tokens per episode with similar observed task success.
